children.title: Extensional Array Regime
children.top_down_role: Array reasoning where elementwise agreement controls array equality.

knowledge_statements.title: Extensional Array Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier-free extensional arrays with read and write operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sorts \(I\) and \(E\), the extensional array theory has sort \(A\), operations \(\operatorname{select}:A\times I\to E\) and \(\operatorname{store}:A\times I\times E\to A\), and satisfies read-over-write: \(\operatorname{select}(\operatorname{store}(a,i,v),i)=v\) and, when \(i\ne j\), \(\operatorname{select}(\operatorname{store}(a,i,v),j)=\operatorname{select}(a,j)\). It also satisfies extensionality: \[\bigl(\forall i\in I,\ \operatorname{select}(a,i)=\operatorname{select}(b,i)\bigr)\Rightarrow a=b.\] Equivalently, \(a\ne b\) implies the existence of an index at which their selected elements differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arrays are equal exactly when all corresponding reads agree; stores obey the usual same-index and different-index read laws.
assumptions_latex: \(I\ne\varnothing\)
\(E\ne\varnothing\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a=b\iff \forall i\in I,\ \operatorname{select}(a,i)=\operatorname{select}(b,i)\)

notation.meaning: Element read from array \(a\) at index \(i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the extensional-array leaf, but no cited source supports the signature, read-over-write axioms, or extensionality equivalence.

children.title: Nonextensional Array Regime
children.top_down_role: Array reasoning without the full extensional equality regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonextensional Array Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arrays governed by read-over-write without observational extensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonextensional array regime uses sorts \(I,E,A\) and operations \(\operatorname{select}\) and \(\operatorname{store}\) satisfying the two read-over-write laws, but it does not impose \[\bigl(\forall i\in I,\ \operatorname{select}(a,i)=\operatorname{select}(b,i)\bigr)\Rightarrow a=b.\] Consequently, models may contain distinct arrays \(a\ne b\) whose selected values agree at every index. Array equality therefore denotes identity in the array domain and is strictly stronger, in some models, than observational agreement under all reads.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Read and write laws hold, but two distinct arrays may return equal elements at every index.
assumptions_latex: \(I\ne\varnothing\)
\(E\ne\varnothing\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists a,b\in A:\ a\ne b\land \forall i\in I,\ \operatorname{select}(a,i)=\operatorname{select}(b,i)\) is permitted

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the nonextensional-array leaf and correctly describes what omitting extensionality permits, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Extensionality Witness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where distinguishing arrays requires witness indices or equivalent solver artifacts.

knowledge_statements.title: Extensionality Witness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite witness instantiation for array disequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each asserted array disequality \(a\ne b\), extensionality may be instantiated with a fresh index constant \(k_{ab}\) and the witness constraint \[\operatorname{select}(a,k_{ab})\ne\operatorname{select}(b,k_{ab}).\] The constant must belong to the common index sort of \(a\) and \(b\), and its reads must participate in all applicable read-over-write and index-equality lemmas. No witness is required merely for an array equality. A reduction omitting a witness for a relevant disequality is not complete for extensional arrays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relevant array disequality needs an index witness whose reads differ and whose index participates in all applicable array lemmas.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b\in A\)
\(a\ne b\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists k_{ab}\in I:\ \operatorname{select}(a,k_{ab})\ne\operatorname{select}(b,k_{ab})\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The witness condition fits the leaf, but the claimed completeness boundary and required participation in all applicable lemmas depend on a specific reduction calculus that is not cited.

children.title: Array Reduction Procedures
children.top_down_role: Reductions translating array constraints into other solver-supported representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Array Reduction Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite reduction of ground array constraints to scalar theory constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite ground conjunction \(F\) over arrays. First flatten every read and write by fresh constants and defining equalities. For each term \(b=\operatorname{store}(a,i,v)\) and each relevant read index \(j\), generate the guarded consequences \(i=j\Rightarrow\operatorname{select}(b,j)=v\) and \(i\ne j\Rightarrow\operatorname{select}(b,j)=\operatorname{select}(a,j)\). For every relevant \(a\ne b\), introduce an extensionality witness and its differing-read constraint. Submit the resulting index and element constraints to their theory solvers. Return satisfiable exactly when the completed reduction is satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flatten array terms, instantiate read-over-write and extensionality lemmas at relevant indices, then solve the resulting index and element constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite and ground
Index and element constraints lie in decidable component theories
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is satisfiable}\iff \operatorname{Red}(F)\text{ is satisfiable}\) under complete instantiation

notation.meaning: Input conjunction of ground array literals.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but “relevant” indices and “complete instantiation” are not formally characterized. A specific array-reduction calculus and adequacy theorem are required to validate the equivalence claim.

children.title: Weak-Equivalence Procedures
children.top_down_role: Array reasoning organized around store chains and weak-equivalence classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Equivalence Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-based propagation through chains of array stores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a graph whose vertices are ground array terms, with unlabeled edges for asserted array equalities and an edge labeled \(i\) between \(a\) and \(\operatorname{store}(a,i,v)\). For reads \(\operatorname{select}(a,j)\) and \(\operatorname{select}(b,k)\), if a path connects \(a\) and \(b\) and the index solver establishes \(j=k\) while establishing that this index differs from every store label on the path, generate \[\operatorname{select}(a,j)=\operatorname{select}(b,k).\] Iterate graph closure, index reasoning, and generated read equalities until no new consequence or a conflict remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A store-chain path transfers read equality when the queried index is equal at both ends and differs from every intervening write index.
assumptions_latex: All array terms and reads are ground
Index equalities and disequalities are decided by the index solver
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\sim_j b\land j=k\Rightarrow \operatorname{select}(a,j)=\operatorname{select}(b,k)\)

notation.meaning: A weak-equivalence path from \(a\) to \(b\) avoiding stores at index \(j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph rule is a plausible weak-equivalence propagation step, but the closure procedure and its completeness depend on the precise weak-equivalence calculus. No source identifies or validates that variant.

children.title: Reduction Adequacy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Fragment and extensionality conditions limiting a chosen array reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Adequacy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions separating equisatisfiable array reductions from incomplete ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A ground reduction is adequate only if it preserves every relevant read-over-write case, propagates equalities through array and index congruence, and supplies a differing-read witness for every relevant extensional array disequality. Under these conditions and complete decision procedures for the index and element theories, the reduced formula is equisatisfiable with the original array formula. Dropping any class can destroy completeness: omitted read cases can miss a store conflict, omitted congruence can miss equal reads, and omitted extensionality witnesses can admit observationally equal arrays asserted disequal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduction is complete only with all relevant store cases, congruence consequences, and extensionality witnesses; omitting any class can admit spurious models.
assumptions_latex: The input formula is finite and ground
Component theory procedures are complete
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ satisfiable}\iff \operatorname{Red}(F)\text{ satisfiable}\) only under complete lemma coverage

notation.meaning: Scalar formula produced by the array reduction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the necessary-and-sufficient coverage claim is calculus-dependent, and the stated assumptions do not precisely define relevance, congruence closure, or component-theory combination requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Lazy Array Lemma Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-guided generation of violated ground array lemmas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a ground array formula \(F\). Solve its current abstraction, initially omitting optional array instances. Inspect the candidate model for violated read-over-write, congruence, or extensionality consequences. If one is violated, add the corresponding ground lemma—introducing a fresh witness index for a violated array disequality when necessary—and solve again. Stop with unsatisfiable when the abstraction is inconsistent; stop with satisfiable when the candidate model satisfies every required array axiom instance over the finite relevant term closure. The output is the final status together with the accumulated lemmas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve an abstraction, add an array lemma violated by its model, and stop when conflict occurs or all required instances hold.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite and ground
The relevant-term closure and component checks are effective
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{status}(F)\in\{\mathsf{sat},\mathsf{unsat}\}\) after lemma saturation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the topic, but termination and satisfiability completeness after finite lemma saturation require a precisely defined relevant-term closure and a cited lazy array-solving procedure.

children.title: Index-Theory Integration
children.top_down_role: Array reasoning coupled to a background theory governing index terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Index-Theory Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling parametric arrays to a solver for their index sort.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the array signature be parameterized by an index theory \(T_I\). Every array lemma whose guard contains index equalities or disequalities is interpreted modulo \(T_I\), not as independent propositional atoms. The array solver communicates relevant index terms and requests consequences such as \(T_I\models i=j\) or \(T_I\models i\ne j\); those consequences select the applicable read-over-write and weak-equivalence cases. Sound integration requires every emitted index constraint to be valid in \(T_I\), while completeness requires deciding every index relation needed by the finite array-lemma closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The index solver decides equalities and disequalities that select store and weak-equivalence cases, with all exchanged constraints interpreted in the index theory.
assumptions_latex: \(T_I\) decides the relevant ground index constraints
Array and index terms are purified at their interface
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_I\models i=j\) or \(T_I\models i\ne j\) determines the applicable guarded array consequence

notation.meaning: Background theory of the array index sort.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits index-theory integration, but completeness generally may require case splitting or equality arrangements rather than the component theory entailing every equality or disequality. A source is needed to fix the exact interface semantics.

children.title: Element-Theory Integration
children.top_down_role: Array reasoning coupled to a background theory governing stored or selected values.

knowledge_statements.title: Element-Theory Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling array reads and stored values to an element theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let array elements belong to a theory \(T_E\). Flattened read terms and stored values are shared with the \(T_E\)-solver, which decides their ground constraints and reports equalities or conflicts implied by \(T_E\). Array reasoning contributes equalities between element terms through read-over-write, congruence, and weak equivalence; \(T_E\) may propagate further consequences back through shared element equalities. Soundness requires purification of mixed terms, and completeness requires that all element equalities relevant to the finite array closure be represented in the combined arrangement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Array lemmas generate element equalities, while the element solver decides their theory-specific consequences and returns relevant equalities or conflicts.
assumptions_latex: \(T_E\) decides relevant ground element constraints
Mixed array-element terms are purified
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_E\cup T_A\models e_1=e_2\) is obtained by complete exchange over shared element terms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits element-theory integration, but “complete exchange” and the conclusion depend on model-combination hypotheses that are not stated or sourced.

children.title: Cross-Sort Combination Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Interaction limits arising when index, element, and array sorts use different theory solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Sort Combination Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface conditions for combining array, index, and element theories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Combination is sound only when mixed terms are purified and all shared index and element terms have consistent equality arrangements across the array solver and component solvers. Completeness additionally requires complete component procedures and exchange of every shared equality needed by array guards or element congruence. A black-box disjoint-signature combination theorem does not apply directly when the array signature uses the component sorts \(I\) and \(E\). If a component admits finite models, lacks stable infiniteness, or shares additional operations, a Nelson–Oppen-style equality exchange requires separate justification or a specialized combination procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared index and element sorts prevent automatic black-box combination; purification, equality exchange, and suitable component-theory hypotheses are required.
assumptions_latex: Array operations have types involving shared sorts \(I\) and \(E\)
Component solvers exchange equalities on shared terms
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Comb}(T_A,T_I,T_E)\) is complete only under justified interface and model-combination conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but the exact effects of shared sorts, stable infiniteness, finite models, and shared operations are combination-framework dependent and require an authoritative theorem with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex-Based Theory Solving
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental feasibility checking for ground linear rational or real constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a conjunction of linear equalities and inequalities over \(D\in\{\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\). Introduce slack variables so each linear form has a defining tableau row and maintain lower and upper bounds on variables. Initialize a tableau assignment satisfying all rows. While some basic variable violates a bound, pivot with an eligible nonbasic variable capable of repairing that violation and update the assignment. If no eligible pivot exists, return unsatisfiable with the conflicting bound combination; otherwise continue until every bound is satisfied and return the resulting assignment. Strict inequalities require an exact symbolic or equivalent sound treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a simplex tableau and bounds, pivot to repair violations, and return either a feasible assignment or a conflicting bound combination.
assumptions_latex: \(D\in\{\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\)
All input constraints are linear with exact coefficients
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le b\text{ is feasible over }D\) or a linear infeasibility certificate is produced

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and tableau outline fit simplex-based SMT theory solving, but the eligible-pivot rule, strict-inequality treatment, termination, and production of a linear infeasibility certificate require a cited algorithm specification.

knowledge_statements.title: Elimination-Based Linear Arithmetic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fourier–Motzkin elimination for linear real-rational feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite system of linear inequalities over \(D\in\{\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\). To eliminate \(x_k\), normalize inequalities with positive coefficient of \(x_k\) as upper bounds and those with negative coefficient as lower bounds; retain inequalities where its coefficient is zero. Combine every lower bound with every upper bound to derive an inequality not containing \(x_k\), then discard the original bounds involving \(x_k\). Repeat until no variable remains or a contradiction such as \(0<0\) is obtained. If the projection is consistent, reconstruct eliminated variables in reverse order and return a feasible assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate each variable by combining every lower bound with every upper bound, detect contradiction, or reconstruct a feasible assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(D\in\{\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\)
The input is a finite system of linear inequalities
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is feasible}\iff \operatorname{FM}(S)\text{ contains no contradictory constant inequality}\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits elimination-based linear arithmetic, but the treatment of strict versus non-strict inequalities and the feasibility/reconstruction equivalence require a cited Fourier–Motzkin theorem or algorithm section.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Arithmetic Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound propagation from nonnegative linear combinations of asserted rational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^m\). If \(c=A^{\mathsf T}\lambda\) and \(\lambda^{\mathsf T}b\le d\), then \(Ax\le b\) implies \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le d\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\); hence the latter bound may be propagated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative combination of asserted inequalities soundly propagates a bound when its combined coefficient vector equals the bound coefficients and its combined right-hand side does not exceed the bound.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), and the current theory literals imply \(Ax\le b\).
\(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le b\Rightarrow c^{\mathsf T}x\le d\).

notation.meaning: Coefficient matrix and right-hand side of asserted linear literals.

children.title: Presburger Arithmetic Fragment

assumptions_latex: Variables and quantified variables range over \(\mathbb{Z}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order additive arithmetic of integers, with congruences admitted as definable shorthand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Presburger arithmetic is the first-order theory of \((\mathbb{Z},0,1,+,<)\). Its formulas are built from Boolean connectives and integer quantifiers applied to linear atoms \(a^{\mathsf T}x\bowtie b\), with \(a\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}\), and \(\bowtie\in\{<,\le,=,\ge,>\}\). children.title: Presburger Elimination Procedures
children.top_down_role: Quantifier-elimination families specialized to Presburger arithmetic.

assumptions_latex: \(\varphi(x,y)\) is a Presburger formula and \(x\) is integer-valued.
All coefficients, bounds, and moduli are normalized to integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(\psi(y)\) satisfies \(\psi(y)\iff\exists x\,\varphi(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: Positive common period of normalized congruence conditions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-variable Cooper-style elimination for existential Presburger formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To eliminate \(x\) from \(\exists x\,\varphi(x,y)\), first remove coefficients of \(x\) by scaling and introduce the required divisibility atoms. Put the formula in a Boolean combination of normalized bounds on \(x\) and congruences modulo positive integers. Let \(M\) be a common multiple of their moduli. Replace the existential search by the finite disjunction over residues \(r\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}\) and the finitely many normalized boundary substitutions prescribed by the lower bounds. Simplify the result to obtain \(\psi(y)\), and iterate for further quantified variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cooper elimination normalizes one integer variable, combines congruence periods, and replaces existential search by finitely many residues and boundary substitutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Presburger Elimination Procedures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for the particular Cooper-style normalization, residue enumeration, and boundary-substitution variant. Those details are variant-sensitive and require an inspectable algorithm or theorem locator.

children.title: Elimination Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural and resource-growth boundaries associated with elimination-based reasoning.

assumptions_latex: A one-variable elimination step explicitly enumerates all residues modulo \(M\).
Moduli are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The elimination step can require \(\Omega(M)=2^{\Omega(L)}\) residue branches.

notation.meaning: Common period used by the elimination step.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-size lower bound for explicit residue enumeration, not optimal Presburger decision complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An elimination procedure that materializes one branch for each residue modulo \(M\) has output size and running time at least \(\Omega(M)\). This is exponential in binary input length: a single congruence with modulus \(M=2^k\) has encoding length \(L=\Theta(k)\), while explicit enumeration creates \(2^k=2^{\Theta(L)}\) branches. With several moduli, replacing \(M\) by their least common multiple can compound this blow-up across successive eliminations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit residue enumeration can be exponential in binary input length, and repeated least-common-multiple construction can amplify elimination blow-up.
knowledge_statements.title: Elimination Complexity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional output-size observation is plausible for an implementation that explicitly materializes every residue, but no source supports the stated asymptotic regime or the claimed compounding across eliminations.

knowledge_statements.title: Diophantine Constraint Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smith-normal-form criterion for solvability of linear Diophantine systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r\), let \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and let unimodular matrices \(U\) and \(V\) satisfy \(UAV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0,\ldots)\), where \(d_i>0\) and \(d_i\mid d_{i+1}\). With \(c=Ub\), the system \(Ax=b\) has a solution in \(\mathbb{Z}^n\) if and only if \(d_i\mid c_i\) for every \(1\le i\le r\) and \(c_i=0\) for every \(r<i\le m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smith normal form reduces integer linear-system feasibility exactly to divisibility conditions on the nonzero diagonal coordinates and zero conditions on the remaining transformed right-hand-side coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=r\).
Unimodular \(U,V\) satisfy \(UAV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0,\ldots)\), where \(d_i>0\) and \(d_i\mid d_{i+1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b\) has a solution in \(\mathbb{Z}^n\) exactly under the displayed divisibility and zero conditions.

notation.meaning: Smith normal form of the integer matrix.

semantic entailment in the background theory

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard soundness interface of lazy SMT and theory-aware search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface invariant shared by eager and lazy coordination of Boolean search with integer arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be the current Boolean assignment and let \(\Gamma(M)\) be its asserted linear-integer theory literals. Coordination may invoke theory reasoning during Boolean propagation and branching or defer some theory checks until a Boolean candidate has formed. Under either schedule, every reported propagation has an explanation \(E\subseteq\Gamma(M)\) satisfying \(E\models_T\ell\), and every reported conflict has an explanation \(C\subseteq\Gamma(M)\) satisfying \(C\models_T\bot\). Every communicated theory cut must be entailed by the current theory context, while every communicated branch must form an exhaustive disjunction for its integer models. These invariants make the resulting learned clauses and pruning steps theory-sound independently of invocation timing.

children.title: Integer-Arithmetic Model Construction

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Arithmetic Model Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain model construction for a conjunction of linear integer constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=\{Ax\le b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) with finite integral bounds, initialize an empty assignment. Repeatedly select an unassigned \(x_i\), compute all integer values in its current propagated interval, and try them in a fixed order. After each choice, propagate linear consequences; if a certified conflict occurs, undo the choice and try the next value. Output the first total assignment \(x^*\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) satisfying every row of \(Ax\le b\). If all values at the root are exhausted through certified conflicts, output UNSAT together with the accumulated search certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate bounded integer values with propagation and certified backtracking. Return a satisfying total assignment, or UNSAT after the finite search tree is exhausted.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(l,u\in\mathbb{Z}^n\).
Every variable has finite bounds \(l_i\le u_i\).
Each pruning step is justified by a valid conflict or propagation explanation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is either \(x^*\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) with \(Ax^*\le b\), or a finite certified exhaustion of all \(x\in[l,u]\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-domain backtracking with sound theory explanations is complete

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is mathematically plausible and its finite-bound hypothesis supplies termination, but no inspectable source supports this particular model-construction procedure or the claimed accumulated search certificate. children.title: Integer-Arithmetic Conflict Explanations
children.top_down_role: Explanatory artifacts supporting integer-arithmetic conflicts.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Arithmetic Conflict Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable theory-conflict clauses for linear integer arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) assert a finite set \(\Gamma(M)\) of linear-integer literals. A conflict explanation is a subset \(C=\{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r\}\subseteq\Gamma(M)\) accompanied by a checkable linear-integer infeasibility certificate establishing \(C\models_{\mathrm{LIA}}\bot\). Its Boolean projection is the clause \(\neg\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg\ell_r\). Because no integer assignment satisfies all members of \(C\), this clause is valid in linear integer arithmetic and may be learned by the Boolean search engine. Minimality of \(C\) is optional and is not required for soundness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible subset of asserted integer-arithmetic literals certifies a learned clause containing their negations. Minimality improves the explanation but is not required.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\ell_j\) denotes a linear constraint or its theory-supported negation over designated integer variables.
The accompanying infeasibility certificate is independently checkable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{LIA}\models\neg\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg\ell_r\).

notation.meaning: linear-integer literals asserted by the current Boolean assignment

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard theory-lemma form for SMT conflict explanations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the conflict-explanation leaf, and the learned-clause consequence is standard and internally consistent. However, no cited source or concrete certificate system establishes what counts as a checkable linear-integer infeasibility certificate.

children.title: Integer-Arithmetic Propagation Explanations
children.top_down_role: Explanatory artifacts supporting theory-implied arithmetic literals.

assumptions_latex: The literals in \(E\cup\{p\}\) have fixed linear-integer semantics.
The infeasibility certificate for \(E\land\neg p\) is independently checkable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{LIA}\models((\ell_1\land\cdots\land\ell_r)\rightarrow p)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable implication explanations for propagated linear-integer literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E=\{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r\}\) be currently asserted linear-integer literals and let \(p\) be an unassigned theory literal. A propagation explanation consists of \(E\), together with a checkable certificate that \(E\land
eg p\) has no integer model. Equivalently, \(E\models_{\mathrm{LIA}}p\). The Boolean clause \(
eg\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor
eg\ell_r\lor p\) is therefore theory-valid and is unit under the current assignment, justifying propagation of \(p\). The explanation remains sound whether or not it is inclusion-minimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: To justify propagating a theory literal, certify that the asserted reasons together with its negation are integer-infeasible; the corresponding implication clause is valid.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Arithmetic Propagation Explanations

children.title: Integer Difference Logic
children.top_down_role: Difference constraints interpreted over integer-valued variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Difference Logic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier-free difference constraints interpreted over integer-valued variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Integer difference logic consists of Boolean combinations of atoms \(x_i-x_j\le c\), where every variable ranges over \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{Z}\). A unary upper bound \(x_i\le c\) is represented as \(x_i-x_0\le c\), and a lower bound \(x_i\ge c\) as \(x_0-x_i\le-c\), using a distinguished variable fixed by \(x_0=0\). A conjunction is satisfiable exactly when there exists \(v:\{x_0,\ldots,x_n\}\to\mathbb{Z}\) satisfying every displayed inequality and \(v(x_0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer difference logic uses inequalities comparing two integer variables. A distinguished zero variable expresses ordinary upper and lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\models x_i-x_j\le c\) if and only if \(v(x_i)-v(x_j)\le c\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of integer difference logic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and integer-domain formulation fit the leaf, and the zero-variable encoding is internally consistent. No inspectable citation with a section, definition, or page locator is supplied, so the record remains source-dependent.

children.title: Rational Difference Logic
children.top_down_role: Difference constraints interpreted over rational-valued variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Difference Logic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier-free difference constraints interpreted over rational-valued variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Rational difference logic consists of Boolean combinations of atoms \(x_i-x_j\le c\), where every variable ranges over \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{Q}\). Introduce a distinguished variable \(x_0\) fixed to zero to write \(x_i\le c\) as \(x_i-x_0\le c\) and \(x_i\ge c\) as \(x_0-x_i\le-c\). A conjunction is satisfiable exactly when some valuation \(v:\{x_0,\ldots,x_n\}\to\mathbb{Q}\), with \(v(x_0)=0\), satisfies every atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational difference logic uses pairwise difference inequalities over rational variables, with a fixed zero variable representing unary bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\models x_i-x_j\le c\) if and only if \(v(x_i)-v(x_j)\le c\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of rational difference logic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and rational-domain formulation fit the leaf, and the zero-variable encoding is internally consistent. No inspectable citation with a section, definition, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Domain-Sensitive Feasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where integer and rational interpretations yield different feasibility or artifact behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Sensitive Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary between rational and integer feasibility for non-strict difference constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a conjunction \(F\) of constraints \(x_i-x_j\le c_{ij}\) with rational constants, rational feasibility is characterized by absence of a negative cycle in the weighted constraint graph. Integer feasibility instead equals feasibility of \(F^{\mathbb Z}\), obtained by replacing every \(c_{ij}\) by \(\lfloor c_{ij}\rfloor\), because integer differences are integral. Consequently rational feasibility need not imply integer feasibility: \(x\le\tfrac12\) and \(-x\le-\tfrac12\) have the rational solution \(x=\tfrac12\), but their rounded integer system requires \(x\le0\) and \(x\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational feasibility uses the original edge weights; integer feasibility uses their floors. A system can therefore have a rational solution but no integer solution.
assumptions_latex: All constraints are non-strict difference inequalities.
Constants are rational and variables share either the rational or integer domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is integer-feasible}\iff F^{\mathbb Z}\text{ is rational-feasible}\), while rational feasibility of \(F\) alone is insufficient.

notation.meaning: system obtained by flooring every right-hand side

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integrality of variable differences permits coefficientwise flooring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate, and coefficientwise flooring is correct for non-strict difference constraints over integer variables. The equivalence also relies on the integral-model property of difference systems with integral weights. Neither that property nor the negative-cycle characterization has an inspectable supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Based Difference Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-cycle decision and shortest-path model construction for conjunctive difference logic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F=\{x_i-x_j\le c_{ij}\}\), construct a directed graph with one vertex per variable and an edge \(j\to i\) of weight \(c_{ij}\). Add a super-source \(s\) with zero-weight edges to every vertex. Run a negative-cycle-detecting shortest-path algorithm. If a negative cycle is found, return its summed inequalities as an infeasibility certificate. Otherwise return shortest-path distances \(d_i\); they satisfy \(d_i-d_j\le c_{ij}\) for every edge. Rational weights yield a rational model, and integral weights yield an integer model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode each difference constraint as a weighted edge. A negative cycle proves infeasibility; otherwise shortest-path distances form a satisfying valuation.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite conjunction of non-strict difference constraints.
Edge weights belong to \(\mathbb{Q}\), or to \(\mathbb{Z}\) when an integer model is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is feasible}\iff G_F\text{ has no negative directed cycle}\).

notation.meaning: weighted constraint graph of the difference system
shortest-path distance assigned to variable vertex i

The cited locator is only a general graph-theory section and is not specific enough to show support for difference-constraint feasibility, certificate extraction, or integer model construction.

children.title: UTVPI Constraints
children.top_down_role: Two-variable-per-inequality constraints with unit coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: UTVPI Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit two-variable-per-inequality constraints over a fixed ordered numerical domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(D\in\{\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R}\}\). A unit two-variable-per-inequality constraint is a linear inequality \(a_ix_i+a_jx_j\le c\) in which at most two distinct variables occur, every nonzero coefficient belongs to \(\{-1,1\}\), and \(c\in D\). Unary constraints \(\pm x_i\le c\) are included by allowing only one nonzero coefficient. A UTVPI system is a finite conjunction of such constraints, interpreted with every variable valued in the same domain \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A UTVPI system contains inequalities with at most two variables, each having coefficient plus or minus one, over a common numeric domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_ix_i+a_jx_j\le c\text{ is UTVPI}\iff a_i,a_j\in\{-1,0,1\}\) and at most two coefficients are nonzero.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of unit two-variable-per-inequality constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf and the main statement gives the usual at-most-two-variable unit-coefficient grammar. The conclusion is only a partial syntactic test because it omits the constant-domain condition, and no inspectable source is supplied. Source-backed clarification is needed before choosing an exact replacement convention.

children.title: Octagonal Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraints represented through octagonal relational structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every defining inequality has the form \(\pm x_i\pm x_j\le c\), with direct unary bounds admitted equivalently.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard syntactic definition of octagonal constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise signed-sum bounds defining an octagonal numerical domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(D\in\{\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R}\}\). An octagonal constraint is an inequality \(s_ix_i+s_jx_j\le c\), where \(s_i,s_j\in\{-1,1\}\), \(c\in D\), and the indices may coincide. With distinct indices it bounds a signed sum or difference of two variables. With coincident indices, equal signs give \(2x_i\le c\) or \(-2x_i\le c\), while opposite signs give a constant constraint. Ordinary unary bounds may equivalently be admitted directly. An octagonal system is a finite conjunction of octagonal constraints interpreted over \(D^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Octagonal systems bound signed sums and differences of pairs of variables. Repeated equal-sign indices or direct unary forms express individual bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Octagonal Constraints

children.title: UTVPI-Octagon Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The representational relationship between UTVPI constraints and octagonal domains.

knowledge_statements.title: UTVPI-Octagon Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntax-preserving correspondence between UTVPI systems and octagonal signed-pair bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Over \(D=\mathbb{Q}\) or \(D=\mathbb{R}\), every binary UTVPI inequality is already an octagonal inequality. Translate a unary inequality \(sx_i\le c\) into the repeated-index octagonal inequality \(sx_i+sx_i\le2c\). Conversely, translate \(sx_i+sx_i\le c\) into \(sx_i\le c/2\). These translations preserve solution sets. Over \(D=\mathbb{Z}\), the reverse repeated-index translation is \(sx_i\le\lfloor c/2\rfloor\); with this rounding convention, solution sets are again preserved. Thus UTVPI and octagonal systems are equivalent presentations of signed one- and two-variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary UTVPI and octagonal inequalities coincide. Unary bounds correspond to repeated-variable octagonal bounds, with floor division required when translating back over integers.
assumptions_latex: All variables use one common domain \(D\in\{\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R}\}\).
Constants belong to \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}_D(F)=\operatorname{Sol}_D(\tau(F))\) for the stated UTVPI-to-octagon translation \(\tau\) and its domain-sensitive inverse.

notation.meaning: a sign in plus or minus one

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct algebraic equivalence of the two constraint grammars

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is the correct role for this correspondence leaf. The stated unary duplication, rational inverse, and integer floor inverse preserve solution sets under the record's conventions. No inspectable source establishes that these are the intended UTVPI and octagonal conventions for this taxonomy, so the correspondence remains source-dependent.

children.title: Cylindrical Algebraic Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Sign-invariant decomposition structures used in nonlinear real arithmetic reasoning.

knowledge_statements.title: Cylindrical Algebraic Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sign-invariant CAD for real polynomial constraints under a fixed variable ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite \(F\subset\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and ordering \(x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_n\), repeatedly apply a sound projection operator to obtain polynomial sets in successively fewer variables. Decompose \(\mathbb{R}\) at the real roots of the univariate projection polynomials, then lift each cell through dimensions \(2,\ldots,n\) using sections at roots and sectors between roots. The output is a finite partition \(\mathcal C\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) into connected semialgebraic cells, cylindrical under coordinate projection, such that every \(f\in F\) has constant sign on each cell. A Boolean combination of sign conditions over \(F\) is decided by evaluating one sample point per cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CAD projects and lifts polynomials to partition real space into cylindrical cells where every input polynomial has constant sign, enabling sample-point evaluation of polynomial formulas.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subset\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is finite.
A sound projection operator and exact real-root isolation are available.
The variable ordering \(x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_n\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a finite cylindrical, sign-invariant decomposition of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) for \(F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm, scope, and content kind are mathematically appropriate, but no inspectable source supports the projection-and-lifting guarantees or sign-invariance conclusion.

children.title: Real Quantifier Elimination
children.top_down_role: Elimination-based treatment of quantified formulas over real closed fields.

knowledge_statements.title: Real Quantifier Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective quantifier elimination for first-order real closed fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every first-order formula \(\varphi(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) over \((\mathbb{R};0,1,+,-,\cdot,<)\), whose atomic predicates are polynomial equalities or inequalities with rational coefficients, there exists an effectively computable quantifier-free formula \(\psi(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) built from polynomial sign conditions such that
\[\mathbb{R}\models\forall y_1\cdots\forall y_m\,\bigl(\varphi(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\leftrightarrow\psi(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\bigr).\]
Consequently, every closed formula in this language is decidable. Cylindrical algebraic decomposition is one algorithmic realization of this elimination result, although quantifier elimination itself does not require that particular implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real closed-field formula with polynomial atoms has an effectively computable equivalent quantifier-free formula; closed formulas are therefore decidable.
assumptions_latex: All polynomial coefficients are rational, or belong to an effectively presented real closed subfield.
The language contains only ordered-field operations and relations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An equivalent quantifier-free \(\psi\) is effectively computable, and every closed \(\varphi\) is decidable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The effective real-closed-field quantifier-elimination theorem is stated correctly, but the theorem and its CAD realization have no cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Projection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Projection choices controlling decomposition structure, retained polynomials, and resource growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for projection operators used by projection-and-lifting CAD.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) map a finite set \(F\subset R[x_1,\ldots,x_k]\) to finitely many polynomials in \(R[x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}]\). For a designated class of inputs, \(P\) is a valid projection regime if every connected base cell \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^{k-1}\) on which all members of \(P(F)\) satisfy the regime's required invariance conditions guarantees that the real roots of polynomials in \(F\) vary over \(C\) without prohibited crossings or multiplicity changes and that lifting over \(C\) produces cells with the required sign, order, or truth invariance. Reduced regimes are valid only when their additional hypotheses, such as well-orientedness or designated equational constraints, hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CAD projection regime is valid when invariant projection data over each base cell guarantees invariant polynomial behavior after lifting; reduced regimes require their side conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is an effective ordered coefficient domain.
\(F\subset R[x_1,\ldots,x_k]\) is finite.
Any side conditions prescribed by the selected regime are checked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lifting above each admissible base cell preserves the invariance promised by the projection regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, but the formulation combines several projection regimes and invariance targets without identifying the precise hypotheses for any one regime. An authoritative source is needed to fix those guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Nonlinear Model Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract incremental SMT loop for quantifier-free nonlinear real constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a quantifier-free conjunction \(A\) of nonlinear real-arithmetic atoms, maintain a relaxation \(R\) and a persistent set \(L\) of sound lemmas. Obtain a candidate assignment \(a\) satisfying \(R\land L\). If no candidate exists, return unsatisfiable. Otherwise, check every atom of \(A\) exactly or with certified bounds at \(a\). If all atoms hold, return \(a\). If some atom fails, derive a lemma \(\ell\) that is valid for the nonlinear theory, excludes \(a\), and is relevant to the failed atom; set \(L\leftarrow L\cup\{\ell\}\) and repeat. Under resource limits, the permitted nondefinitive result is unknown.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver repeatedly tests relaxed candidate models, returns a verified model, or adds sound nonlinear lemmas excluding invalid candidates; without completeness guarantees it may return unknown.
assumptions_latex: Each learned lemma is valid in the intended nonlinear theory.
A reported model is checked against every original atom.
The relaxation solver is sound for \(R\land L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A returned model satisfies \(A\), and an unsatisfiable result is valid when \(R\land L\) is a sound overapproximation of \(A\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits, but sound UNSAT requires the invariant that the original formula implies the maintained relaxation and lemmas. That relation is not imposed before the unconditional UNSAT return, and solver architectures vary materially.

children.title: Interval Constraint Propagation
children.top_down_role: Domain narrowing over interval representations for nonlinear real constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Constraint Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound box contraction for nonlinear real constraints using inclusion-monotone interval extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=I_1\times\cdots\times I_n\) be an interval box and let \(g_j(x)\in S_j\) be constraints with interval extensions \([g_j]\). Initialize \(B^{(0)}=B\). Repeatedly apply sound contractors \(C_j\) satisfying \(C_j(D)\subseteq D\) and
\[\{x\in D:g_j(x)\in S_j\}\subseteq C_j(D).\]
Stop at an empty box, a common fixed point, or a prescribed contraction threshold. Return the contracted box \(B'\). If \(B'=\varnothing\), the original box contains no feasible point; otherwise every feasible point originally in \(B\) remains in \(B'\), but nonemptiness alone does not certify feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval propagation repeatedly contracts a box without removing feasible points. An empty result certifies infeasibility, while a nonempty fixed point need not contain a solution.
assumptions_latex: Each \([g_j]\) encloses the range of \(g_j\) on every processed box.
Every contractor \(C_j\) is contracting and solution-preserving.
Interval endpoints use outward-rounded or exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B'\subseteq B\) and every feasible point of \(B\) lies in \(B'\); \(B'=\varnothing\) certifies local infeasibility.

children.title: Branching Search Regimes
children.top_down_role: Partitioning choices used to explore unresolved nonlinear interval regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Search Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound branch-and-prune search over bounded real boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a bounded initial box \(B_0\) and constraints \(F\), maintain a worklist initialized with \(B_0\). Select a box \(B\), apply sound interval contractors, and discard it if contraction proves infeasibility. If a certified point in \(B\) satisfies \(F\), return that point. Otherwise choose a coordinate \(i\) and split value \(c\in\operatorname{int}(I_i)\), form children whose union is \(B\), and enqueue them. Under a finite stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), unresolved boxes of width at most \(\varepsilon\) are returned as unknown or as explicitly defined approximate witnesses, never as exact models without certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch-and-prune contracts boxes, discards certified-infeasible boxes, accepts certified models, and bisects unresolved boxes. Tolerance-sized boxes remain approximate unless a separate model certificate exists.
assumptions_latex: \(B_0\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is bounded.
Contractors never remove feasible points.
Every split covers its parent box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Definitive infeasible and feasible outputs are sound; tolerance termination alone yields only an approximate or unknown result.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The branch-and-prune algorithm and its distinction between certified and tolerance-based outputs are appropriate, but no cited source supports this search contract or its termination boundary.

children.title: Interval Precision Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where interval overapproximation limits decisiveness or artifact strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Precision Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of finite-precision interval exclusion and tolerance-based termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inclusion interval extension \([f]\), the test \(0\notin[f](B)\) soundly excludes roots of \(f(x)=0\) from \(B\). The converse fails: \(0\in[f](B)\) need not imply that a root exists, because dependency and rounding may overestimate the range. Moreover, stopping when \(\operatorname{wid}(B)\leq\varepsilon\) yields only an \(\varepsilon\)-localized unresolved box unless existence is separately certified. For example, natural interval evaluation of \(f(x)=x-x+1\) on \(B=[0,1]\) gives \([f](B)=[0,2]\), which contains zero although \(f(x)=1\) everywhere. Thus finite precision and interval inclusion alone cannot justify exact satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval exclusion is one-sided: containing zero does not prove a root. Dependency can create false uncertainty, and small unresolved boxes are not exact satisfiability certificates.
assumptions_latex: \([f](B)\) is an inclusion extension of the real range of \(f\) on \(B\).
The stopping tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in[f](B)\) or \(\operatorname{wid}(B)\leq\varepsilon\) does not, by itself, certify an exact root.

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of the range of f on B

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear-Integer Decidability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between bounded nonlinear integer search and unrestricted Diophantine satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For integer variables restricted to explicitly bounded finite domains, satisfiability of any effectively evaluable finite collection of polynomial equalities and inequalities is decidable by exhaustive enumeration. In contrast, there is no algorithm that, for every polynomial \(p\in\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) with arbitrary \(n\), decides whether
\[\exists x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq0}\quad p(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0.\]
Hence unrestricted quantifier-free nonlinear integer arithmetic containing multiplication of variables is undecidable in general. Decidable fragments require restrictions such as finite bounds, linearity, or another independently established decision procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded nonlinear integer constraints are decidable by finite enumeration, but unrestricted existential polynomial equations over nonnegative integers are undecidable, so general nonlinear integer arithmetic has no complete solver.
assumptions_latex: Polynomial coefficients are integers.
The undecidable fragment permits an unbounded number of nonnegative integer variables and variable multiplication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded finite-domain instances are decidable, whereas unrestricted existential Diophantine satisfiability is undecidable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-enumeration and unrestricted Diophantine-undecidability boundary is correctly stated, but the DPRM/Hilbert's tenth theorem requires an authoritative citation with a theorem, section, or page locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Nonlinear-Integer Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound three-outcome contract for heuristic nonlinear-integer reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a procedure for a nonlinear integer formula \(\varphi\) that may return \(\mathsf{sat}\), \(\mathsf{unsat}\), or \(\mathsf{unknown}\). Sound incompleteness requires: a \(\mathsf{sat}\) result includes an integer assignment \(a\) whose substitution makes every atom of \(\varphi\) true; an \(\mathsf{unsat}\) result is supported by a checkable contradiction or a sound reduction proving that no integer model exists; and whenever neither condition is established, the procedure returns \(\mathsf{unknown}\). Because unrestricted nonlinear integer satisfiability is undecidable, no terminating procedure can satisfy these soundness requirements while always avoiding \(\mathsf{unknown}\) on the full fragment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incomplete nonlinear-integer solver may answer sat or unsat only with sound justification; otherwise it returns unknown. No terminating complete procedure exists for the unrestricted fragment.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\) belongs to a nonlinear integer fragment containing an undecidable Diophantine subfragment.
The procedure terminates on every input.
Definitive outputs are required to be sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some inputs must yield \(\mathsf{unknown}\), although every reported \(\mathsf{sat}\) or \(\mathsf{unsat}\) result remains valid.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three-outcome soundness principle and unavoidable-unknown conclusion are appropriate, but both the solver contract and the underlying undecidability result lack cited support.

knowledge_statements.title: Transcendental-Function Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decidability loss when polynomial real arithmetic is extended by unrestricted sine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Quantifier elimination for real closed fields does not automatically extend to formulas containing transcendental functions. In particular, suppose the language contains integer-coefficient polynomials, a constant \(\pi\), and unrestricted \(\sin\). The constraint \(\sin(\pi x)=0\) holds exactly when \(x\in\mathbb{Z}\). Therefore any existential Diophantine equation \(p(x_1,
\ldots,x_n)=0\) can be represented over real variables by
\[p(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\ \land\ \bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}\sin(\pi x_i)=0.\]
A decision procedure for all such real formulas would decide Hilbert's tenth problem. Hence satisfiability for this unrestricted transcendental extension is undecidable; restricted domains or certified approximations require separately stated guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unrestricted sine can force real variables to be integers, embedding Diophantine equations. Thus real polynomial arithmetic extended with sine and pi is undecidable in general.
assumptions_latex: The language contains unrestricted real \(\sin\) and the exact constant \(\pi\).
Existential formulas may contain arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomials.
Variables range over all real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Satisfiability of the stated transcendental extension is undecidable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sine-based reduction is mathematically plausible for the explicitly stated signature containing exact pi and unrestricted sine, but this signature-sensitive undecidability claim needs an authoritative locator.

children.title: Signed Bit-Vector Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Bit-vector operations interpreted through signed numeric conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Signed Bit-Vector Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two's-complement interpretation of a fixed-width bit vector as an integer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For width \(w\geq1\), let \(b=(b_{w-1},\ldots,b_0)\in\{0,1\}^{w}\), with \(b_{w-1}\) the most significant bit. Its signed two's-complement value is
\[\operatorname{sbv}_w(b)=-2^{w-1}b_{w-1}+\sum_{i=0}^{w-2}2^i b_i.\]
Equivalently, if \(u=\sum_{i=0}^{w-1}2^i b_i\) is the unsigned value, then \(\operatorname{sbv}_w(b)=u\) when \(u<2^{w-1}\), and \(\operatorname{sbv}_w(b)=u-2^w\) otherwise. Thus the representable signed range is exactly \([-2^{w-1},2^{w-1}-1]\cap\mathbb{Z}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A width-w vector denotes its unsigned value below the sign threshold and that value minus two to the w otherwise, giving the standard two's-complement range.
assumptions_latex: \(w\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(w\geq1\).
Each bit \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sbv}_w\) maps \(\{0,1\}^w\) bijectively onto \([-2^{w-1},2^{w-1}-1]\cap\mathbb{Z}\).

notation.meaning: unsigned value of the same bit pattern

children.title: Unsigned Bit-Vector Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Bit-vector operations interpreted through unsigned numeric conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsigned Bit-Vector Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positional unsigned interpretation of a fixed-width bit vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For width \(w\geq1\), let \(b=(b_{w-1},\ldots,b_0)\in\{0,1\}^{w}\), where \(b_0\) is the least significant bit. Its unsigned value is
\[\operatorname{ubv}_w(b)=\sum_{i=0}^{w-1}2^i b_i.\]
This map is a bijection from \(\{0,1\}^{w}\) to \(\{0,1,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). Consequently, fixed-width addition and multiplication interpreted as bit-vector operations correspond to integer addition and multiplication reduced modulo \(2^w\); unsigned comparisons correspond to the ordinary order on these representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A width-w vector denotes the binary positional value from zero through two to the w minus one; fixed-width arithmetic is arithmetic modulo two to the w.
assumptions_latex: \(w\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(w\geq1\).
Each bit \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ubv}_w\) bijectively represents residues by integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), with bit-vector arithmetic reduced modulo \(2^w\).
