children.title: Fixed-Width Regimes
children.top_down_role: Semantic variation induced by declared bit-vector widths.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Width Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the modular semantics of one fixed positive bit width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed integer width \(w\ge 1\), the bit-vector domain is \(\mathbb B_w=\{0,1\}^w\). Its unsigned value map is \(U_w(b_{w-1}\cdots b_0)=\sum_{i=0}^{w-1}2^i b_i\). Arithmetic operations returning width \(w\) are interpreted modulo \(2^w\); hence addition and multiplication satisfy \(U_w(x+y)=\bigl(U_w(x)+U_w(y)\bigr)\bmod 2^w\) and \(U_w(xy)=\bigl(U_w(x)U_w(y)\bigr)\bmod 2^w\). Equality compares all \(w\) bits, while signed or unsigned order is selected separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-width bit vector has exactly w bits, and its width-preserving arithmetic wraps modulo 2^w; signedness affects interpretation and ordering, not its bit pattern.
assumptions_latex: \(w\in\mathbb N\) and \(w\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb B_w\) is closed under width-preserving modular arithmetic.

notation.meaning: set of bit vectors of width w

review_flags: Authoritative fixed-size bit-vector semantics source and exact locator are missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Fixed-Width Regimes leaf and is mathematically standard, with consistent delimited notation. However, no citation or inspectable locator is supplied for the fixed-size bit-vector domain, modular arithmetic semantics, or separation of signed and unsigned ordering. Source support is required before candidate review can accept it.

children.title: Width Conversion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Truncation, extension, extraction, and concatenation behavior across differing widths.

knowledge_statements.title: Width Conversion Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when truncation and extension preserve interpreted values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb B_w\). Zero extension to width \(v\ge w\) preserves \(U_w(x)\), and sign extension preserves the two's-complement value \(S_w(x)\). Truncation to \(v<w\) preserves only the low \(v\) bits and has unsigned value \(U_v(\operatorname{trunc}_v(x))=U_w(x)\bmod 2^v\). Thus truncation preserves unsigned value exactly iff \(U_w(x)<2^v\), and preserves signed value exactly iff \(-2^{v-1}\le S_w(x)<2^{v-1}\). Outside these ranges, conversion changes the interpreted integer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension preserves value only under the matching signedness convention. Narrowing discards high bits and preserves an integer exactly only when that integer fits the target range.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb B_w\) and \(v\ge 1\).
Signed values use two's-complement interpretation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Narrowing is value-preserving exactly on the representable target range.

notation.meaning: two's-complement signed interpretation at width w
retention of the least significant v bits

review_flags: Authoritative bit-vector conversion source and exact locator are missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the stated zero-extension, sign-extension, truncation, and representable-range conditions are precise under two's-complement semantics. No authoritative conversion-semantics source or exact locator is supplied, so the exact iff boundaries remain unsupported.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Blasting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an equisatisfiable Boolean encoding of quantifier-free fixed-size bit vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a quantifier-free fixed-size bit-vector formula \(F\). Associate each width-\(w\) variable with Boolean bits \(x_0,\ldots,x_{w-1}\). Recursively replace every bit-vector operator by a Boolean circuit implementing its fixed-width semantics, and connect shared subterms to fresh gate variables using definitional constraints. Encode bit-vector equality as bitwise equivalence and predicates as their comparator circuits. Convert the resulting circuit to CNF with a satisfiability-preserving gate encoding, producing \(C_F\). Return satisfiable exactly when the SAT solver finds a Boolean assignment satisfying \(C_F\); decode the variable bits as a model of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bit-blasting replaces words and word operators by Boolean bits and circuits, then solves the resulting equisatisfiable SAT instance and decodes any model.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is quantifier-free and every bit-vector sort has fixed finite width.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is satisfiable if and only if \(C_F\) is satisfiable.
review_flags: A source establishing equisatisfiability of the standard bit-blasting translation is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind for Bit-Blasting, and the record states the intended equisatisfiable translation for quantifier-free fixed-size bit vectors. Acceptance requires a source with a specific section or theorem supporting the operator-to-circuit translation, satisfiability-preserving CNF encoding, and model decoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Word-Level Bit-Vector Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the soundness obligation for reasoning before Boolean expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a fixed-size bit-vector formula. A word-level reasoning step may replace \(F\) by \(F'\), or add a lemma \(L\), only when fixed-width bit-vector semantics validates \(F\leftrightarrow F'\), or respectively \(F\models L\). Such steps may use modular identities, interval information, extraction and concatenation rules, and congruence over whole words without exposing every bit. Consequently, any sequence of validated word-level transformations preserves satisfiability, and any generated lemma is satisfied by every bit-vector model of the current formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Word-level reasoning manipulates whole bit vectors using valid modular and structural identities; each rewrite must preserve satisfiability and each learned lemma must follow semantically.
assumptions_latex: All operators have fixed-width bit-vector semantics.
Every rewrite or lemma schema used is semantically valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validated word-level transformations preserve satisfiability and produce sound lemmas.

notation.meaning: bit-vector formulas before and after a transformation

review_flags: The node admits several solver architectures; a canonical word-level reasoning reference is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role is plausible for the broad Word-Level Bit-Vector Reasoning container, and its semantic soundness obligation is coherent. The node covers multiple solver architectures, however, and no cited source fixes or supports this particular collection of word-level techniques and transformation obligations.

children.title: Lazy Bit-Blasting
children.top_down_role: Deferred Boolean encoding of selected bit-vector constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Lazy Bit-Blasting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies demand-driven Boolean expansion with theory-consistent refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a quantifier-free bit-vector formula \(F\). Initialize a Boolean abstraction \(A_0\) in which selected word-level atoms or operations remain abstract. At iteration \(k\), obtain a SAT assignment \(M_k\) for \(A_k\). If \(M_k\) extends to a fixed-width bit-vector model of \(F\), return that model. Otherwise select an inconsistent abstract operation or atom, generate a sound Boolean encoding or conflict lemma \(R_k\) excluding \(M_k\), and set \(A_{k+1}=A_k\land R_k\). Return unsatisfiable when the abstraction is unsatisfiable. Full finite expansion guarantees termination if refinement remains incomplete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lazy bit-blasting expands only portions needed to reject spurious Boolean assignments, stopping with a bit-vector model or an unsatisfiable refined abstraction.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is quantifier-free over fixed finite widths.
Each refinement is sound and excludes the current spurious assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure is sound; it is complete when refinement can reach the full bit-level encoding.
review_flags: Lazy bit-blasting variants differ; a source fixing this abstraction-refinement formulation is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the Lazy Bit-Blasting leaf, but lazy bit-blasting has materially different abstraction and refinement formulations. Moreover, the sentence claiming that full finite expansion guarantees termination "if refinement remains incomplete" is unclear: termination normally requires a progress or fairness condition ensuring that refinement can eventually reach a complete finite encoding. A source is needed to determine the intended algorithm and correct completeness hypothesis.

children.title: Incremental Bit-Blasting
children.top_down_role: Bit-blasting organized for evolving solver contexts and repeated checks.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Bit-Blasting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines monotone extension of a retained SAT encoding across solver calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a sequence of contexts \(F_0,F_1,\ldots\), maintain a SAT solver and a persistent mapping from each encountered bit-vector subterm to its Boolean circuit variables. For each new assertion, bit-blast only previously unseen subterms, add their gate clauses and the assertion's activation-guarded clauses, and solve under assumptions selecting the active context. On a push, retain all clauses and mappings; on a pop, deactivate clauses belonging exclusively to the removed context rather than deleting shared encodings. The returned SAT result and decoded model must correspond exactly to the assertions active in the selected context.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental bit-blasting retains Boolean circuits and learned SAT state, adds encodings only for new terms, and uses guards or assumptions to select the active context.
assumptions_latex: Each context contains quantifier-free fixed-size bit-vector assertions.
Activation guards correctly characterize context membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each solver result is equisatisfiable with the currently active bit-vector context.

notation.meaning: bit-vector assertion context at stage i

review_flags: An authoritative source for incremental bit-blasting and activation semantics is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for Incremental Bit-Blasting, and the active-context correctness obligation is stated. No source or exact locator supports the specific persistent-mapping, activation-guard, push/pop, and learned-state formulation, so its claimed context semantics cannot yet be accepted.

children.title: Encoding Reuse Across Contexts
children.top_down_role: Persistence and reuse of generated Boolean structure across incremental contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Reuse Across Contexts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when cached bit-level encodings remain valid after context changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t\) be a fixed-width bit-vector subterm occurring in contexts \(F_i\) and \(F_j\). A cached Boolean encoding \(E(t)\) may be reused in both contexts when the sort, width, operator semantics, operand-to-bit mapping, and defining gate clauses for \(t\) are identical. Clauses encoding context-specific assertions must instead be guarded or scoped. Under these conditions, sharing \(E(t)\) preserves the models of each active context and introduces no cross-context constraint except the common semantics of \(t\). Reuse is invalid if widths, interpretations, or mapped operands differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bit-level encoding can be shared across contexts only when the term and all semantic parameters match; context-specific constraints require separate scoping or guards.
assumptions_latex: The cached encoding is definitional for the represented subterm.
Context-specific clauses are correctly guarded or scoped.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reusable definitional encodings preserve each active context's model set.

notation.meaning: cached Boolean encoding of subterm t

review_flags: A source documenting precise cache-reuse invariants across incremental contexts is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is an appropriate role for the conditions governing Encoding Reuse Across Contexts. The proposed invariants are plausible, but no inspectable source establishes that this list is sufficient, especially where solver-local gate variables, definitions, and scoped clauses interact across contexts.

children.title: Array-Coupled Bit Vectors
children.top_down_role: Bit-vector reasoning combined with array indices, elements, or array-encoded memories.

knowledge_statements.title: Array-Coupled Bit Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the combined semantics of arrays indexed by or storing bit vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\mathbb B_m\), \(V=\mathbb B_n\), and let an array \(a\) denote a total function \(I\to V\). Selection and storage satisfy \(\operatorname{select}(\operatorname{store}(a,i,v),j)=v\) when \(i=j\), and \(\operatorname{select}(\operatorname{store}(a,i,v),j)=\operatorname{select}(a,j)\) when \(i\ne j\). Equality of indices is fixed-width bit-vector equality, while values returned by selection retain width \(n\). For extensional arrays, \(a=b\) holds exactly when \(\operatorname{select}(a,i)=\operatorname{select}(b,i)\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An array-coupled bit-vector model treats arrays as total maps between finite bit-vector domains, combining read-over-write and extensionality with fixed-width index and value semantics.
assumptions_latex: Arrays use extensional total-function semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Array operations and bit-vector operations share equality through finite-width indices and values.
review_flags: Authoritative combined array and fixed-size bit-vector theory source is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the Array-Coupled Bit Vectors leaf. The total-function, read-over-write, fixed-width equality, and extensionality semantics are internally consistent, but no source with a precise locator supports the combined array and bit-vector interpretation.

children.title: Arithmetic-Coupled Bit Vectors
children.top_down_role: Bit-vector reasoning combined with integer or real arithmetic representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic-Coupled Bit Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates fixed-width words to bounded integer arithmetic through explicit conversion maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For width \(w\ge1\), couple \(x\in\mathbb B_w\) to an integer \(z\) by either \(z=U_w(x)\) with \(0\le z<2^w\), or \(z=S_w(x)\) with \(-2^{w-1}\le z<2^{w-1}\). Under unsigned coupling, width-preserving addition corresponds to \(U_w(x+y)=\bigl(U_w(x)+U_w(y)\bigr)\bmod 2^w\); analogous congruences hold for other modular operations. Ordinary integer arithmetic agrees with bit-vector arithmetic only when its result lies in the chosen representable range or when the required modular reduction is stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bit vectors couple to integers through signed or unsigned conversion plus range constraints; arithmetic agrees only within range or after explicit modular reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb B_w\) and \(w\ge1\).
The signedness of every conversion is fixed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupling is exact only with its range constraints and modular arithmetic semantics.
review_flags: Authoritative mixed integer and bit-vector conversion semantics source is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is suitable for Arithmetic-Coupled Bit Vectors, and the record correctly distinguishes signed and unsigned range constraints from modular word arithmetic. No authoritative mixed integer/bit-vector conversion source or exact locator is provided to support the stated coupling and agreement boundary.

children.title: Mixed-Theory Conversion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Semantic and representational limits at bit-vector, array, and arithmetic interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Theory Conversion Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies unsound crossings between bit-vector and neighboring theory semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conversion boundary between \(x\in\mathbb B_w\) and another theory is semantics-preserving only if width, signedness, range, and overflow behavior are explicit. Mapping to integers requires \(z=U_w(x)\) or \(z=S_w(x)\) with the corresponding range constraint. Mapping an integer \(z\) back to width \(w\) yields its residue modulo \(2^w\), not generally \(z\). Likewise, array indices converted between integers and bit vectors alias whenever their integers are congruent modulo \(2^w\). Omitting these constraints can admit models forbidden by the source theory or discard valid modular models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-theory conversions are reliable only when width, signedness, ranges, and wraparound are explicit; otherwise integer values may alias or disagree with bit-vector values.
assumptions_latex: Conversions connect fixed-size bit vectors with integer arithmetic or array indexing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unconstrained conversions need not preserve satisfiability or models.
review_flags: A source covering precise mixed-theory conversion and aliasing boundaries is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct role for this leaf. The modular aliasing warning is plausible, but the claim spans integer conversion, array indexing, model preservation, and satisfiability effects without a source fixing the exact mixed-theory semantics. A precise citation is required.

children.title: Floating-Point Formats
children.top_down_role: Precision and exponent-width regimes governing floating-point values.

knowledge_statements.title: Floating-Point Formats
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines binary floating-point values by exponent and significand widths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary floating-point format is determined by exponent width \(e\ge2\) and significand precision \(p\ge2\), and is written \(\mathbb F_{e,p}\). Its encodings contain one sign bit, \(e\) exponent bits, and \(p-1\) explicit trailing-significand bits. Exponent and significand fields encode finite normal and subnormal numbers; reserved exponent patterns encode signed infinities and NaNs. The format also distinguishes positive and negative zero. Thus \(\mathbb F_{e,p}\) is a finite semantic domain whose values, exceptional classes, precision, and exponent range depend on \((e,p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary floating-point format fixes exponent and precision widths, thereby determining its finite numbers, signed zeros, infinities, NaNs, range, and precision.
assumptions_latex: \(e,p\in\mathbb N\), \(e\ge2\), and \(p\ge2\).
The encoding follows IEEE-style binary interchange semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((e,p)\) determines the floating-point domain \(\mathbb F_{e,p}\).

notation.meaning: binary floating-point domain with exponent width e and precision p

review_flags: An IEEE 754 or SMT-LIB floating-point format locator is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits Floating-Point Formats, and the parameterization is consistent with the SMT-LIB convention in which significand width includes the implicit leading bit. Because conventions for precision and explicit fraction width vary, an IEEE 754 or SMT-LIB citation with a specific section is necessary to validate the exact encoding and exceptional-value claims.

children.title: Rounding Modes
children.top_down_role: Rounding-direction regimes affecting floating-point operation results.

knowledge_statements.title: Rounding Modes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the five standard rounding directions used by floating-point operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a floating-point format \(\mathbb F_{e,p}\), a rounding mode selects a representable result for an exact real result lying between adjacent floating-point numbers. The standard modes are round to nearest with ties to even, round to nearest with ties away from zero, round toward positive infinity, round toward negative infinity, and round toward zero. For finite exact \(r\), each directed mode chooses the nearest representable value in its prescribed direction, while a nearest mode minimizes distance and applies its stated tie rule. Floating-point arithmetic operators are therefore functions of both operands and the selected rounding mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rounding mode maps an exact result to a format value using nearest-even, nearest-away, upward, downward, or toward-zero behavior, including a specified rule for ties.
assumptions_latex: A binary floating-point format \(\mathbb F_{e,p}\) is fixed.
The exact result is interpreted under IEEE-style rounding semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rounding mode uniquely determines the prescribed rounded result, subject to exceptional-value rules.

notation.meaning: exact finite real result before rounding

review_flags: An IEEE 754 or SMT-LIB rounding-mode locator is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct role for Rounding Modes, and the five listed modes match the usual SMT floating-point taxonomy. A precise IEEE 754 or SMT-LIB locator is still required because uniqueness and directed-rounding behavior depend on overflow, signed-zero, infinity, and exceptional-result rules that the statement only qualifies generally.

children.title: Exceptional Floating-Point Values
children.top_down_role: NaNs, infinities, signed zeros, and related exceptional-value distinctions.

assumptions_latex: A floating-point format has exponent width \(e\ge 2\) and significand precision \(p\ge 2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exceptional values are precisely the two infinities, signed zeros, and NaNs encoded by the format.

notation.meaning: Floating-point format with exponent width e and precision p.
The set of NaN values in the format.

review_flags: A floating-point standard or SMT floating-point theory specification with an exact exceptional-value locator is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: IEEE-style binary floating-point values as represented in SMT floating-point theories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the binary floating-point format \(F_{e,p}\), define its exceptional-value set by \[E_{e,p}=\{+\infty,-\infty,+0,-0\}\cup\operatorname{NaN}_{e,p}.\] A NaN has an all-ones exponent field and a nonzero trailing-significand field; an infinity has an all-ones exponent and a zero trailing-significand field; and a signed zero has zero exponent and trailing-significand fields. Distinct NaN bit patterns may denote distinct representable values at the encoding level, although ordinary floating-point equality is false whenever either operand is NaN.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exceptional floating-point values comprise positive and negative infinity, positive and negative zero, and all NaN encodings; equality involving NaN is false.
knowledge_statements.title: Exceptional Floating-Point Values

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the exceptional-value classification or equality semantics. The statement also needs an authoritative distinction between semantic NaN values in SMT floating-point theory and multiple NaN bit-pattern encodings.

children.title: Format-Sensitive Exceptional Behavior
children.top_down_role: Interactions among format width, rounding choice, and exceptional-value outcomes.

assumptions_latex: Two binary formats \(F_{e,p}\) and \(F_{e',p'}\) may have different exponent ranges or precisions.
Each operation uses a specified rounding mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exceptional outcomes can change when the same real inputs and operation are evaluated in different formats.

notation.meaning: Rounding of a real value into format F under rounding mode r.
Largest finite positive value of format F.
Smallest positive normal value of format F.

review_flags: A floating-point standard or SMT floating-point theory specification with format-dependent overflow, underflow, and NaN rules is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of exceptional results on exponent range, precision, and rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\circ\) be a real arithmetic operation and let \(r\) be a rounding mode. The floating-point result in format \(F\) is determined by \(\operatorname{rnd}_{F,r}(x\circ y)\), together with the format's exceptional-operation rules. If a finite exact result has magnitude exceeding \(M_F\), overflow may produce an infinity or a maximal finite value according to \(r\); if its magnitude lies below \(m_F^{\mathrm N}\), it may become subnormal or signed zero. Consequently, changing \(F\) can alter finiteness, normality, zero sign, and NaN propagation even when \(x\), \(y\), \(\circ\), and \(r\) are otherwise fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing exponent width or precision can turn the same exact computation into a finite value, subnormal, signed zero, infinity, or NaN.
knowledge_statements.title: Format-Sensitive Exceptional Behavior

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the format-dependent overflow, underflow, zero-sign, or NaN claims. In particular, the assertion that changing only the format can alter NaN propagation for fixed real operands and one operation requires qualification and authoritative support.

assumptions_latex: The input is a quantifier-free floating-point formula over fixed finite formats.
All floating-point operations and predicates have bit-vector encodings matching their specified semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated bit-vector formula is satisfiable exactly when the original floating-point formula is satisfiable.

notation.meaning: Bit-vector encoding of a floating-point formula.
Exponent width and significand precision of a format.

review_flags: An SMT floating-point reduction specification or solver paper with a precise soundness and completeness statement is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eager bit-blasting of fixed-format, quantifier-free floating-point formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a quantifier-free formula \(\varphi\) over fixed formats \((e,p)\). Encode each floating-point variable by its sign, exponent, and trailing-significand bit-vectors. Replace every constructor, classification predicate, comparison, conversion, and rounded arithmetic operation by a bit-vector circuit implementing the prescribed exceptional cases and rounding mode. Conjoin any auxiliary circuit constraints and output \(\mathcal B(\varphi)\). The reduction is bit-precise when \[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable in floating-point semantics}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal B(\varphi)\text{ is satisfiable in bit-vector semantics}.\] A satisfying bit-vector assignment is decoded fieldwise into a floating-point model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode every fixed-format floating-point value and operation as bit-vectors and circuits, preserving satisfiability in both directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Precise Floating-Point Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the reduction container, but its bidirectional satisfiability claim depends on exact encodings of every supported operation, conversion, predicate, rounding mode, and exceptional case. No specification or soundness/completeness locator is cited.

children.title: Floating-Point Abstraction
children.top_down_role: Coarser representations used to reason about floating-point constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the concrete domain of fixed-format floating-point states.
\(A\) is an abstract domain ordered by precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The abstract semantics overapproximates all concrete floating-point behaviors.

notation.meaning: Concrete and abstract transformers for an operation f.

review_flags: A source defining a sound abstraction specifically for floating-point SMT reasoning is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound overapproximation used in floating-point abstraction-refinement solving.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A floating-point abstraction consists of an abstract domain \((A,\sqsubseteq)\), an abstraction map \(\alpha:\mathcal P(C)\to A\), and a concretization map \(\gamma:A\to\mathcal P(C)\) satisfying \(S\subseteq\gamma(\alpha(S))\) for every \(S\subseteq C\). For each concrete floating-point transformer \(f_C\), its abstract transformer \(f_A\) is sound when \[f_C(\gamma(a))\subseteq\gamma(f_A(a))\qquad\text{for every }a\in A.\] Thus an abstract model may include behaviors absent from the exact format, but no concrete behavior permitted by the original formula is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A floating-point abstraction maps concrete states into an ordered domain whose transformers include every behavior of the exact floating-point operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Floating-Point Abstraction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is a standard abstract-interpretation soundness pattern, but no source establishes this formulation or its specialization to fixed-format floating-point SMT reasoning.

children.title: Floating-Point Refinement
children.top_down_role: Precision strengthening used after an abstract result proves insufficient.

assumptions_latex: An abstract floating-point formula has a candidate model \(m_A\).
Exact fixed-format validation can determine whether \(m_A\) has a concrete realization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each refinement preserves concrete solutions while excluding the rejected abstract candidate or its infeasible region.
review_flags: A source specifying a sound floating-point abstraction-refinement loop and its progress conditions is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample-guided refinement for quantifier-free fixed-format floating-point constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(k=0\) with a sound abstraction \(\Phi_A^0\) of the concrete formula \(\Phi\). Solve \(\Phi_A^k\). If it is unsatisfiable, return unsatisfiable. Otherwise validate its model \(m_A^k\) against exact floating-point semantics. If validation yields a concrete model, return satisfiable with that model. If validation fails, construct \(R_k\) such that every concrete model of \(\Phi\) satisfies \(R_k\) while \(m_A^k\not\models R_k\), set \(\Phi_A^{k+1}=\Phi_A^k\land R_k\), increment \(k\), and repeat. Termination additionally requires a finite refinement space or another well-founded progress argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve an overapproximation, validate its candidate exactly, and add a sound constraint excluding each unrealizable candidate until a result is obtained.
knowledge_statements.title: Floating-Point Refinement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local role are appropriate, but the soundness of abstract unsatisfiability, candidate validation, refinement preservation, and the stated termination condition require a cited floating-point abstraction-refinement result.

children.title: Spurious Floating-Point Candidates
children.top_down_role: Abstract candidates that fail under bit-precise floating-point semantics.

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi_A\) soundly overapproximates a concrete floating-point formula \(\Phi\).
\(m_A\) satisfies \(\Phi_A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An abstract candidate \(m_A\models\Phi_A\) is spurious with respect to \(\Phi\) precisely when \[\gamma(m_A)\cap\operatorname{Mod}_C(\Phi)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, the exact floating-point validation formula obtained by fixing or constraining abstract observations according to \(m_A\) is unsatisfiable. Soundness of the abstraction implies that abstract unsatisfiability certifies concrete unsatisfiability, but abstract satisfiability alone does not certify concrete satisfiability. A spurious candidate therefore witnesses imprecision of the abstraction rather than inconsistency of the original concrete theory.

assumptions_latex: Datatype constructors are free and their result sorts are fixed.
Datatype values are finite constructor trees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constructor disjointness, injectivity, selector behavior, and acyclicity characterize free datatype reasoning.

notation.meaning: Constructors of a datatype sort D.
Selector corresponding to the j-th argument of constructor c_i.

review_flags: An SMT-LIB datatype theory specification or authoritative datatype-decision-procedure source with exact locators is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order reasoning over freely generated finite algebraic datatypes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a free datatype sort \(D\) generated by constructors \(c_i\), distinct constructors have disjoint ranges, and each constructor is injective: \[c_i(\bar x)\neq c_j(\bar y)\text{ for }i\neq j,\qquad c_i(\bar x)=c_i(\bar y)\Longrightarrow\bar x=\bar y.\] For every constructor argument, \(s_{ij}(c_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n))=x_j\). Every value of \(D\) is denoted by a finite constructor term, so no value is a proper constructor subterm of itself. Selector values on terms built by nonmatching constructors are governed by the theory's chosen totalization convention and are not fixed by freeness alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free datatype reasoning uses disjoint and injective constructors, matching selectors, exhaustive finite construction, and exclusion of cyclic constructor terms.
knowledge_statements.title: Free Datatype Reasoning

children.title: Recursive Datatypes
children.top_down_role: Datatype families containing self-referential constructor structure.

assumptions_latex: A datatype declaration contains at least one constructor whose argument refers directly or indirectly to its own result sort.
The declaration satisfies a nonemptiness or well-foundedness condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The datatype denotes the least set closed under its constructors, containing only finite well-founded values.

notation.meaning: Polynomial-like constructor operator induced by the declaration.

review_flags: An authoritative source for SMT recursive datatype semantics and admissibility conditions is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-fixed-point semantics of a single inductive recursive datatype.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recursive datatype \(D\) is interpreted as the least fixed point of the constructor operator \(F\): \[D\cong\mu X.\,F(X).\] Concretely, \(D\) is the least carrier closed under every declared constructor, where recursive constructor arguments range over \(D\). Hence every member of \(D\) has a finite, well-founded constructor-tree representation, and structural induction is valid: if a predicate holds for each constructor result whenever it holds for all recursive arguments, then it holds for every value in \(D\). A declaration with no finite constructor-generated value does not define a nonempty inductive datatype under this semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recursive datatype is the least constructor-closed set, so all its values are finite well-founded trees and support structural induction.
knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Datatypes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The least-fixed-point definition fits the container, but the admissibility and nonemptiness conditions for recursive SMT datatype declarations are not specified precisely or supported by a source.

children.title: Mutually Recursive Datatypes
children.top_down_role: Datatype families whose constructor structure creates recursion across multiple sorts.

knowledge_statements.title: Mutually Recursive Datatypes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous least-fixed-point semantics for finite mutually recursive datatype families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mutually recursive datatype family \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\) is interpreted by the simultaneous least fixed point \[(D_1,\ldots,D_n)\cong\mu(X_1,\ldots,X_n).\,(F_1(\bar X),\ldots,F_n(\bar X)).\] Each \(F_i\) is induced by the constructors returning sort \(D_i\), and constructor arguments may use any carrier in the family. Every value is a finite well-founded tree whose nodes are constructors and whose child sorts follow the declarations. Induction is simultaneous: predicates \(P_i\) hold on all \(D_i\) when every constructor preserves the appropriate predicate from each recursive argument to its result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mutually recursive datatypes are the simultaneous least solution of linked constructor equations and consist of finite, sort-correct constructor trees.
assumptions_latex: A finite family of datatype declarations may refer to one another through constructor arguments.
The family has a well-defined nonempty simultaneous least fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The carriers are interpreted simultaneously as the least solution of their constructor equations.

notation.meaning: Datatype carriers in a mutually recursive family.
Constructor operators induced by the declarations.

review_flags: An authoritative source for simultaneous least-fixed-point semantics of mutually recursive SMT datatypes is required.

children.title: Datatype Dependency Topologies
children.top_down_role: Dependency structures distinguishing isolated recursion, mutual cycles, and acyclic references.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many datatype sorts and constructor declarations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strongly connected components identify mutually recursive blocks, and their condensation graph gives a valid dependency order.

notation.meaning: Strongly connected component containing sort D.

review_flags: A source connecting datatype declarations, dependency graphs, and mutually recursive blocks is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph representation of direct, indirect, and mutual datatype recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent datatype dependencies by the directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), where \(V\) is the set of datatype sorts and \((D_i,D_j)\in E\) exactly when a constructor returning \(D_i\) has an argument whose sort contains \(D_j\). A directed cycle denotes recursive dependence; a self-loop denotes direct recursion. Two sorts are mutually recursive exactly when they lie in the same nontrivial strongly connected component, or share a singleton component with a self-loop. Contracting every strongly connected component yields an acyclic condensation graph, whose topological orders are valid orders for processing the mutually recursive declaration blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed sort-dependency graph exposes direct recursion, cycles, mutually recursive components, and an acyclic order between those components.
knowledge_statements.title: Datatype Dependency Topologies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph representation and content kind fit the topology leaf, but no source supports the chosen dependency-edge convention or its correspondence with mutually recursive declaration blocks.

children.title: Codatatype Semantics
children.top_down_role: Potentially infinite constructor structures interpreted through codatatype semantics.

assumptions_latex: Constructors are free and may generate infinite observations.
Equality is extensional with respect to all finite constructor observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A codatatype is the greatest fixed point of its constructor functor and may contain infinite values.

notation.meaning: Constructor functor induced by a codatatype declaration.

review_flags: An authoritative SMT codatatype semantics source with an exact greatest-fixed-point locator is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greatest-fixed-point semantics with equality by finite observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A codatatype \(C\) is interpreted as the greatest fixed point of its constructor functor \(F\): \[C\cong\nu X.\,F(X).\] Its elements may therefore be finite or infinite constructor trees, subject to the sort and constructor declarations. Destructor observations expose one constructor layer at a time. Two values \(x,y\in C\) are equal exactly when no finite sequence of constructor tests and destructor observations distinguishes them; equivalently, equality is the largest bisimulation compatible with the constructors. Unlike an inductive datatype, \(C\) is not restricted to well-founded constructor trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A codatatype is a greatest fixed point containing potentially infinite constructor trees, with equality determined by all finite observations or bisimulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Codatatype Semantics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the container, but greatest-fixed-point semantics, inclusion of finite trees, observational equality, and equivalence with largest bisimulation require an authoritative codatatype source with a precise locator.

children.title: Productivity Reasoning
children.top_down_role: Reasoning about whether codatatype observations can continue to expose constructor structure.

assumptions_latex: A corecursive specification defines a value of a codatatype.
Each recursive call is syntactically or semantically guarded by a constructor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite observation of the specified value can be computed after finitely many unfoldings.

notation.meaning: Observation of x through at most n constructor layers.

review_flags: An authoritative source relating guarded corecursion to productivity for codatatypes is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guarded-corecursion criterion for productivity of codatatype definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A corecursive codatatype definition is productive when, for every finite depth \(n\in\mathbb N\), the observation \(\operatorname{obs}_n(x)\) is obtained after finitely many evaluation steps. A sufficient guardedness condition is that every cyclic path from a defining equation back to a recursive call passes through a constructor that emits one observable layer before the call is demanded. Under this condition, unfolding can always reveal the next constructor in finite time, so the definition determines a unique codatatype value by its compatible family of finite observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A corecursive definition is productive when every finite observation is computable in finite time; constructor-guarded recursive calls provide a sufficient criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Productivity Reasoning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits productivity reasoning, but the stated guarded-cycle criterion and the conclusion that it determines a unique codatatype value depend on the evaluation and corecursion formalism. No supporting source is cited.

children.title: Finite Observation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of distinguishing infinite codatatype values through finite observations.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a codatatype with finite-depth observation maps \(\pi_n:C\to O_n\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).
The observation family \((\pi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is separating.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(x,y\in C\), \(x=y\iff \forall n\in\mathbb N,\;\pi_n(x)=\pi_n(y)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: separating finite observations give the standard extensional equality principle for codatatypes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-depth observations characterize equality when the observation family is separating.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a codatatype and, for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(\pi_n:C\to O_n\) expose observations through depth \(n\). Assume the family \((\pi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is separating. Then, for all \(x,y\in C\),
\[
x=y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall n\in\mathbb N,\;\pi_n(x)=\pi_n(y).
\]
Consequently, unequal elements have a finite observation boundary: if \(x\ne y\), then some \(n\in\mathbb N\) satisfies \(\pi_n(x)\ne\pi_n(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For separating observations, two codatatype values are equal exactly when every finite-depth observation agrees; any inequality is exposed at some finite depth.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Observation Boundaries

children.title: Datatype Cardinality Reasoning
children.top_down_role: Finite or infinite cardinality behavior of datatype sorts relevant to satisfiability.

knowledge_statements.title: Datatype Cardinality Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinalities of mutually recursive free datatypes are least fixed points of constructor polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider finitely many mutually recursive datatype sorts \(D_1,\ldots,D_m\). For each constructor \(c:D_{j_1}\times\cdots\times D_{j_r}\to D_i\), let its argument sorts be recorded with multiplicity. Under free-datatype semantics, the cardinal vector \(\boldsymbol\kappa=(|D_1|,\ldots,|D_m|)\) is the least cardinal fixed point of
\[
F_i(\boldsymbol\kappa)=\sum_{c:\,\operatorname{res}(c)=D_i}\prod_{q=1}^{r_c}\kappa_{j_q}.
\]
Thus emptiness, finiteness, and infinitude can be inferred by solving the induced monotone cardinal equations from the zero vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mutually recursive free datatype has the least cardinalities satisfying the sum-of-products equations induced by its constructors.
assumptions_latex: The signature contains finitely many free constructors of finite arity.
Datatype carriers use initial-algebra semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\boldsymbol\kappa=\operatorname{lfp}(F)\).

notation.meaning: Cardinality of the carrier of D_i

children.title: Datatype Theory Combination

knowledge_statements.title: Datatype Theory Combination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combination requires both equality arrangements and compatible shared-sort cardinalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let quantifier-free constraints \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) belong to theories \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) with disjoint nonlogical signatures and shared variables \(V
e\varnothing\). A combination is satisfiable precisely when there exist an equality arrangement \(E\) on \(V\), component models \(M_i\models_{T_i}\varphi_i\land E\), and, for every shared sort \(S\), a cardinal \(\kappa_S\) such that both \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) admit expansions with \(|S|=\kappa_S\). For datatype sorts, the admissible \(\kappa_S\) must also satisfy their constructor-induced cardinal constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint theories combine only when they agree on shared equalities and admit common carrier cardinalities, including datatype cardinality restrictions.

\(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) are quantifier-free constraints sharing variables only through common sorts.

children.title: Stable-Infiniteness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cardinality-sensitive limits affecting modular combination with datatype sorts.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Infiniteness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite datatypes violate the stable-infiniteness hypothesis used by ordinary Nelson–Oppen combination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A theory \(T\) is stably infinite on a shared sort \(S\) when every satisfiable quantifier-free \(T\)-formula has a \(T\)-model in which \(S\) is infinite. A datatype theory containing the exhaustive nullary constructors \(\mathsf{false}:B\) and \(\mathsf{true}:B\), with distinctness and exhaustiveness, forces
\[
|B|=2.
\]
Hence it is not stably infinite on \(B\). Equality-arrangement exchange alone is therefore not a generally complete combination method when such a finite datatype sort is shared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exhaustive two-constructor Boolean datatype has exactly two elements, so its theory is not stably infinite and ordinary equality-only combination may fail.
assumptions_latex: The datatype sort \(B\) has exactly the distinct nullary constructors \(\mathsf{false}\) and \(\mathsf{true}\).
The sort \(B\) is shared with another theory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|B|=2\), so the datatype theory is not stably infinite on \(B\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stable infiniteness is precluded by a shared sort whose axioms force finite cardinality

children.title: Shared-Sort Cardinality Interaction
children.top_down_role: Interaction between datatype cardinalities and constraints contributed by combined theories.

assumptions_latex: The component signatures are disjoint apart from shared sorts and equality.
Each set \(K_{i,j}\) is computed relative to the same shared-variable arrangement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_i K_{i,j}=\varnothing\) implies combination unsatisfiability; witnessed common members certify cardinal compatibility.

notation.meaning: Cardinalities theory i can realize for shared sort j
Selected common cardinality for shared sort j

effectiveness and sufficiency conditions need authoritative sourcing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common cardinal assignment certifies compatibility of component models on shared sorts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For component theories \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) sharing sorts \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\), let \(K_{i,j}\) be the set of cardinalities realizable for \(S_j\) by a model of the current \(T_i\)-constraints and shared equality arrangement. A cardinality-compatibility certificate is a tuple \((\kappa_1,\ldots,\kappa_m)\) satisfying
\[
\kappa_j\in\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}K_{i,j}\qquad(1\le j\le m).
\]
If some intersection is empty, the component constraints cannot have models with matching shared carriers. If all memberships are witnessed by component models, the tuple certifies cardinal compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible component models require a cardinality for every shared sort that each theory can realize under the chosen equality arrangement.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Sort Cardinality Interaction

knowledge_statements.title: Word-Equation Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Word equations are equalities between concatenation terms interpreted in a free monoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a finite variable set \(X\). A word equation is an equality
\[
U=V,
\]
where \(U,V\in(\Sigma\cup X)^*\). A solution is a substitution \(\sigma:X\to\Sigma^*\), extended uniquely to a monoid homomorphism \(\sigma:(\Sigma\cup X)^*\to\Sigma^*\) that fixes every letter of \(\Sigma\), such that \(\sigma(U)=\sigma(V)\). A finite system is solvable when one substitution satisfies every equation simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A word equation equates two concatenation expressions; a solution assigns finite words to variables so that both instantiated sides are identical.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma\) and \(X\) are finite and disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma\) solves \(U=V\iff \sigma(U)=\sigma(V)\).

notation.meaning: Free monoid of finite words over the alphabet

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard free-monoid definition of a word equation and its solution

knowledge_statements.title: Regular-Language Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular membership restricts a string term to the language recognized by a finite automaton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t\) be a string term over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), and let \(A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,I,F)\) be a finite automaton. The regular-language constraint \(t\in L(A)\) holds under an assignment \(\sigma\) exactly when there exist \(n\in\mathbb N\), letters \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\Sigma\), and states \(q_0,\ldots,q_n\in Q\) such that \(\sigma(t)=a_1\cdots a_n\), \(q_0\in I\), \(q_n\in F\), and \(q_j\in\delta(q_{j-1},a_j)\) for every \(1\le j\le n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular-language constraint holds when the assigned string labels an accepting path through the specified finite automaton.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite automaton over the finite alphabet \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma\models t\in L(A)\iff \sigma(t)\) labels an accepting run of \(A\).

children.title: String-Length Constraints
children.top_down_role: Length terms, bounds, plus consistency conditions arising from string constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: String-Length Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: String length is the unique concatenation-to-addition homomorphism sending each letter to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), the length map \(|\cdot|:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb N\) satisfies
\[
|\varepsilon|=0,\qquad |a|=1\ \text{for every }a\in\Sigma,\qquad |uv|=|u|+|v|.
\]
Therefore every word equation \(U=V\) entails the arithmetic equality \(|U|=|V|\). A string-length constraint is an arithmetic predicate over terms \(|t|\), interpreted in \(\mathbb N\); its solutions must satisfy both the string semantics of \(t\) and the induced arithmetic predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Length maps empty words to zero and concatenation to addition; equal strings necessarily have equal lengths, enabling arithmetic constraints on string terms.
assumptions_latex: Strings are finite words in \(\Sigma^*\).
Arithmetic length values range over \(\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=V\Rightarrow |U|=|V|\), with \(|uv|=|u|+|v|\).

notation.meaning: Length of the interpreted string term t

children.title: Arithmetic Combination Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces linking string-derived length facts to arithmetic solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Combination Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Length variables and bridge equations form the interface between string and arithmetic solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given string terms \(t_1,\ldots,t_r\), introduce fresh arithmetic variables \(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r\) and bridge constraints
\[
\ell_i=|t_i|\land \ell_i\ge 0\qquad(1\le i\le r).
\]
For each syntactic identity \(t_i=t_jt_k\), add \(\ell_i=\ell_j+\ell_k\); for \(t_i=\varepsilon\), add \(\ell_i=0\). Replacing every arithmetic occurrence of \(|t_i|\) by \(\ell_i\), while retaining the bridge constraints, preserves satisfiability. The arithmetic projection is necessary but need not alone characterize realizable string assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fresh nonnegative length variables, linked to string terms and concatenation, provide a satisfiability-preserving interface to an arithmetic solver.
assumptions_latex: Every string term whose length occurs arithmetically receives a fresh length variable.
Bridge constraints retain the semantic equalities \(\ell_i=|t_i|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bridged formula is satisfiable iff the original mixed formula is satisfiable.

children.title: Mixed String–Arithmetic Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed String–Arithmetic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit finite length bounds yield a decidable mixed string–arithmetic regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi\) be a quantifier-free formula over finite strings on a finite alphabet and arithmetic variables. Suppose its string atoms are word equations or regular-language memberships, its arithmetic atoms belong to a decidable theory over \(\mathbb N\), and arithmetic constraints imply a computable bound \(|x|\le B_x\) for every string variable \(x\). Then satisfiability of \(\Phi\) is decidable: enumerate the finite product
\[
\prod_x\{w\in\Sigma^*:|w|\le B_x\},
\]
check all string atoms, and decide the residual arithmetic formula for each assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed string–arithmetic satisfiability is decidable when arithmetic supplies a computable finite length bound for every string variable.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma\) and the set of string variables are finite.
Every string variable has a computable arithmetic-implied upper length bound.
The residual arithmetic theory is decidable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Satisfiability of \(\Phi\) is decidable by finite string enumeration and arithmetic decision.

children.title: Decidable String Fragments

knowledge_statements.title: Decidable String Fragments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential word equations with regular membership constraints form a decidable fragment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Sigma\) be a finite alphabet. Given word equations \(U_i=V_i\) for \(1\le i\le m\) and regular constraints \(x_j\in L(A_j)\) for \(1\le j\le r\), where all variables range over \(\Sigma^*\) and every \(A_j\) is a finite automaton, it is decidable whether there exists a substitution \(\sigma\) satisfying
\[
\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}\sigma(U_i)=\sigma(V_i)\quad\land\quad
\bigwedge_{j=1}^{r}\sigma(x_j)\in L(A_j).
\]
Thus existential conjunctions of word equations and regular membership constraints have decidable satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existential systems of word equations augmented with finite-automaton membership constraints have a decidable satisfiability problem.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma\) and the equation system are finite.
Every side constraint is membership in a regular language represented by a finite automaton.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existential satisfiability of word equations with regular constraints is decidable.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete String-Solver Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded model search is incomplete for proving unsatisfiability without a complete cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a procedure that, for bounds \(B=0,1,2,\ldots\), enumerates assignments with \(|x|\le B\) and returns satisfiable upon finding a model, but returns unsatisfiable only when supplied a proved complete cutoff. This procedure is incomplete on unbounded formulas. For example, over an alphabet containing \(a\), the equation
\[
x=ax
\]
has no solution in finite words because it would imply \(|x|=1+|x|\). Nevertheless, failure to find a model at any particular finite bound does not constitute the procedure's required global unsatisfiability certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded enumeration finds finite models but cannot generally prove unbounded unsatisfiability; the unsatisfiable equation x = ax exposes this limitation.
assumptions_latex: String variables range over finite words.
The search procedure has no proved global length cutoff for the input formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded search without a complete cutoff is not a decision procedure for unbounded string constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Undecidable String Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expressiveness boundary for extensions of finite-string constraint languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a string-constraint language with an effective interpretation over \(\Sigma^*\). Suppose there is a computable map \(M\mapsto\varphi_M\) from Turing machines to closed \(L\)-formulas such that \(\varphi_M\) is satisfiable exactly when \(M\) halts on blank input. Then satisfiability for \(L\) is undecidable. Consequently, any string extension capable of uniformly defining this halting computation—through unrestricted iteration, transitive closure, or an equivalent mechanism—lies beyond complete terminating SMT decision procedures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A string theory becomes undecidable whenever its added operators can uniformly encode whether an arbitrary Turing machine halts.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma\) is a finite alphabet.
The translation \(M\mapsto\varphi_M\) is computable.
Satisfiability of \(\varphi_M\) is equivalent to halting of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SAT}(L)\) is undecidable.

notation.meaning: set of finite words over the alphabet

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the reduction criterion is mathematically standard. However, no inspectable citation supports either the reduction claim or the assertion that the listed extension mechanisms uniformly encode halting computations; those examples require fragment-specific sources.

children.title: Sequence Theory Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraint families over finite sequences of general element sorts.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence Theory Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Many-sorted first-order constraints over finite sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an element sort \(E\), the sequence domain is \(E^*=\bigcup_{n\ge 0}E^n\). A sequence-theory constraint is a first-order formula constructed from equality, the empty sequence \(\epsilon\), singleton construction \(\operatorname{unit}:E\to E^*\), concatenation \(\mathbin{\cdot}:E^*\times E^*\to E^*\), length \(|\cdot|:E^*\to\mathbb N\), and optionally indexed selection. Their semantics satisfy \(|\epsilon|=0\), \(|s\cdot t|=|s|+|t|\), and \((s\cdot t)[i]=s[i]\) for \(0\le i<|s|\), with the analogous shifted rule for \(|s|\le i<|s|+|t|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequence constraints reason about finite ordered collections using emptiness, singleton construction, concatenation, length, equality, and optionally bounded indexing.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a nonempty first-order element domain.
Indexed selection is constrained to indices \(0\le i<|s|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s,t\in E^*\Longrightarrow s\cdot t\in E^*\text{ and }|s\cdot t|=|s|+|t|\).

notation.meaning: element at zero-based valid index i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role and finite-sequence semantics fit the container. No source reference or specific locator is supplied for the signature, indexing convention, or semantic equations.

children.title: String–Sequence Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Representational links between character strings, generic sequences, plus their solver interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: String–Sequence Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical identification of strings with finite character sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma\) be an alphabet and let \(\operatorname{Seq}(\Sigma)\) denote finite sequences of symbols from \(\Sigma\). The map \(\iota:\Sigma^*\to\operatorname{Seq}(\Sigma)\), defined by \(\iota(a_1\cdots a_n)=\langle a_1,\ldots,a_n\rangle\), is a bijection. It preserves the monoid structure and length: \(\iota(\varepsilon)=\langle\rangle\), \(\iota(uv)=\iota(u)\mathbin{\cdot}\iota(v)\), and \(|\iota(u)|=|u|\). Thus formulas using equality, concatenation, constants, and length translate compositionally between strings and character sequences while preserving satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A string is canonically a finite character sequence; the correspondence preserves emptiness, concatenation, length, equality, and satisfiability.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma\) is the common character domain.
Both structures use finite objects and standard concatenation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\iota:\Sigma^*\cong\operatorname{Seq}(\Sigma)\) is a length-preserving monoid isomorphism.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the correct role, and the stated bijection and preservation properties are coherent for the specified common alphabet. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required for the correspondence and satisfiability-preserving translation claim.

children.title: Specialized SMT Theories
children.top_down_role: Additional established theory families whose detailed development belongs in specialized logic or algebra chapters.

children.title: Finite Set Constraints
children.top_down_role: SMT reasoning over finite set values and set operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Set Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional constraints over finite subsets of an element domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a domain \(U\), a finite-set value is a subset \(S\subseteq U\) with finite cardinality. Finite-set constraints are first-order formulas over such values using equality, membership, subset, union, intersection, difference, insertion, deletion, and cardinality, interpreted extensionally. In particular, \(S=T\) exactly when \(\forall x\in U\,(x\in S\leftrightarrow x\in T)\), and \(|S|=\sum_{x\in U}\mathbf 1_S(x)\), where the sum is finite because \(S\) has finite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-set constraints describe finite extensional subsets using membership, Boolean set operations, subset relations, and cardinality.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a nonempty element domain.
Every set-valued variable denotes a finite subset of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=T\Longleftrightarrow \forall x\in U\,(x\in S\leftrightarrow x\in T)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition accurately describes finite extensional sets and fits the leaf. The record has no inspectable citation for the theory signature, extensional semantics, or cardinality interpretation.

children.title: Finite Bag Constraints
children.top_down_role: SMT reasoning over finite multisets with multiplicity-sensitive operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Bag Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite multisets represented by finitely supported multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a domain \(U\), a finite bag is a function \(B:U\to\mathbb N\) whose support \(\{x\in U:B(x)>0\}\) is finite. Bag equality is pointwise equality; membership means \(B(x)>0\); cardinality is \(|B|=\sum_{x\in U}B(x)\). Standard bag operations are defined pointwise by \((B\uplus C)(x)=B(x)+C(x)\), \((B\cap C)(x)=\min\{B(x),C(x)\}\), and \((B\setminus C)(x)=\max\{B(x)-C(x),0\}\). Finite-bag constraints are formulas over these operations and multiplicity comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite bag assigns each element a natural-number multiplicity, with finite support; bag operations act pointwise on multiplicities.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a nonempty element domain.
Bag multiplicity functions have finite support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|B|=\sum_{x\in U}B(x)<\infty\).

notation.meaning: multiplicity of x in bag B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, and the finitely supported multiplicity model and pointwise operations are internally consistent. No source with a specific definition or section locator is provided.

children.title: Finite Relation Constraints
children.top_down_role: SMT reasoning over finite relations and relational operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Relation Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraints over finite sets of ordered tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For domains \(U_1,\ldots,U_k\), a finite \(k\)-ary relation is a finite subset \(R\subseteq U_1\times\cdots\times U_k\). Relation constraints use extensional equality, tuple membership, union, intersection, difference, projection, selection, and, for compatible binary relations, converse and composition. For \(R\subseteq U\times V\) and \(S\subseteq V\times W\), composition is \(S\circ R=\{(u,w):\exists v\in V\,((u,v)\in R\land(v,w)\in S)\}\). The result is finite whenever \(R\) and \(S\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-relation constraints treat relations as finite tuple sets and support relational operations such as projection, converse, and composition.
assumptions_latex: All relation-valued variables denote finite relations.
Composition is applied only to relations with compatible component domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R,S\text{ finite}\Longrightarrow S\circ R\text{ finite}\).

notation.meaning: relational composition, applying R before S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the finite-relation leaf, and the typed composition formula is mathematically coherent. The claimed theory operations and finiteness property lack an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Collection-Theory Interoperability
children.top_down_role: Conversions, shared representations, plus mixed constraints across finite collection theories.

knowledge_statements.title: Collection-Theory Interoperability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantics-preserving embeddings among finite sets, bags, and relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a domain \(U\), embed a finite set \(S\) into bags by \(e(S)(x)=1\) if \(x\in S\) and \(0\) otherwise, and embed a finite binary relation \(R\subseteq U\times V\) into sets by \(p(R)=\{\langle x,y\rangle:(x,y)\in R\}\). These embeddings are injective and preserve extensional equality, membership, emptiness, intersection, and cardinality. Set union corresponds to pointwise maximum under \(e\), not additive bag union; therefore interoperability constraints must distinguish idempotent set union from multiplicity-adding bag union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite sets embed as zero-one bags, and finite relations as sets of tuples; shared operations transfer, but additive bag union differs from set union.
assumptions_latex: Ordered pairs are available in the element universe.
Bag multiplicities range over \(\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(S\cup T)(x)=\max\{e(S)(x),e(T)(x)\}\) and \(e\) is injective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is appropriate for this interoperability leaf. The zero-one bag and tuple-set embeddings are coherent, including the distinction between maximum-based set union and additive bag union, but no source supports the combined preservation claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order field constraints over a fixed finite carrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite field is a finite set \(F\) equipped with operations \(+\) and \(\cdot\) and constants \(0,1\), where \((F,+,0)\) is an abelian group, \((F\setminus\{0\},\cdot,1)\) is an abelian group, and multiplication distributes over addition. Its cardinality is \(q=p^n\) for a prime \(p\) and integer \(n\ge1\); conversely, a field of order \(p^n\) exists and is unique up to isomorphism. Finite-field SMT constraints are polynomial equalities and disequalities interpreted in a fixed such field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite field satisfies the field axioms on finitely many elements, has prime-power order, and interprets polynomial constraints modulo its field operations.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite and \(0\ne1\).
The operations satisfy the field axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|F|=p^n\) for some prime \(p\) and integer \(n\ge1\).

notation.meaning: finite field of order q, up to isomorphism

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is a plausible role for the broad topic, but the record also asserts the prime-power classification, existence, and uniqueness theorem. Those nontrivial claims and the stated SMT interpretation require an authoritative source with specific locators before the mathematical package can be reviewed reliably.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Logic Fragments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heap semantics for separating conjunction and restricted decidable fragments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let heaps be finite partial maps \(h:A\rightharpoonup V\). For assertions \(P,Q\), separating conjunction is defined by \(h\models P*Q\) exactly when there exist heaps \(h_1,h_2\) with disjoint domains such that \(h=h_1\uplus h_2\), \(h_1\models P\), and \(h_2\models Q\). The assertion \(\operatorname{emp}\) holds exactly on the empty heap, and \(x\mapsto v\) holds on the singleton heap mapping \(x\) to \(v\). A separation-logic fragment restricts formulas, predicates, or quantification while retaining this heap-splitting semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation logic interprets separating conjunction by splitting a finite heap into disjoint parts satisfying the component assertions.
assumptions_latex: Heaps are finite partial maps.
The disjoint union \(h_1\uplus h_2\) is defined only for disjoint domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\models P*Q\Longleftrightarrow\exists h_1,h_2\,(h=h_1\uplus h_2\land h_1\models P\land h_2\models Q)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The heap-splitting semantics is a suitable definition for the topic, but the record does not identify any particular separation-logic fragment or its restrictions. No inspectable source is supplied for the points-to semantics or the fragment characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order SMT Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SMT syntax extended with typed functions as first-class values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A higher-order SMT extension admits simple types generated from base sorts by function types \(\sigma\to\tau\), together with typed application and optionally lambda abstraction. Under standard semantics, a term \(f:\sigma\to\tau\) denotes a total function, application \(f\,a\) denotes its value at \(a\), and equality at function type is extensional: \(f=g\) exactly when \(\forall x:\sigma\,(f\,x=g\,x)\). Satisfiability asks for interpretations of base sorts, theory symbols, and higher-order variables satisfying the closed formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order SMT permits functions as values, typed application, and possibly lambdas, with function equality interpreted extensionally.
assumptions_latex: Terms are well typed in a simple type system.
Function denotations are total.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g\Longleftrightarrow\forall x:\sigma\,(f\,x=g\,x)\) for \(f,g:\sigma\to\tau\).

notation.meaning: type of total functions from σ to τ

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the topic, and the statement consistently describes a simply typed, total-function, extensional semantics. Higher-order SMT formalisms differ on lambda abstraction and equality treatment, so a specific authoritative semantics source and locator are required.

children.top_down_role: Architectures connecting propositional search, theory decision procedures, preprocessing, state management, and model construction.
