knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite ground clause set \(G\), collect the extension terms occurring in \(G\), instantiate \(K\) to obtain \(K[G]\), and replace each ground extension term by a fresh constant. Add defining equations and the congruence constraints required for equal arguments to yield equal extension values. Invoke a decision procedure for \(T_0\) on the purified clauses. Under locality, report satisfiable exactly when the resulting base-theory problem is satisfiable; otherwise report unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local theory extension is combined with its base theory by finite axiom instantiation, purification, congruence constraints, and base-theory solving.
knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Extension Combination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm describes a standard locality-based reduction, but the precise definition of K[G], purification obligations, and congruence constraints depends on the theory-extension framework. A source is also needed to justify placing this locality-specific algorithm in the broader Theory-Extension Combination leaf.

children.title: Shared-Signature Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility requirements imposed by symbols shared across component signatures.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M_i\models T_i\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\).
\(\Sigma_0=\Sigma_1\cap\Sigma_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility requires the \(\Sigma_0\)-reducts of the component models to admit embeddings into one common \(\Sigma_0\)-structure that preserves all shared symbols.

notation.meaning: Shared-signature reduct of the component model
Embeddings into a common shared structure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic compatibility condition for component models with a nontrivial common signature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The component models are shared-signature compatible if there exist a \(\Sigma_0\)-structure \(\mathcal A\) and embeddings \(e_i:\mathcal M_i\upharpoonright_{\Sigma_0}\to\mathcal A\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\) such that the embedded reducts agree on identified interface elements. If combination requires a common carrier rather than an amalgam, compatibility strengthens to an isomorphism \(h:\mathcal M_1\upharpoonright_{\Sigma_0}\cong\mathcal M_2\upharpoonright_{\Sigma_0}\). Absence of the required amalgam or isomorphism blocks combined-model construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component models are compatible when their shared-signature reducts can be embedded into one common structure, or identified isomorphically when carriers must coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Signature Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Embeddings into an arbitrary common structure do not by themselves specify how interface elements are identified or guarantee an amalgam. The required compatibility notion varies by framework, so its mathematical formulation cannot be settled without a source.

children.title: Extension-Locality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Locality regimes controlling reduction from extension reasoning to base-theory reasoning.

knowledge_statements.title: Extension-Locality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the prescribed finite ground-instantiation reduction for a theory extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed instance-selection operator \(G\mapsto K[G]\), locality requires that every finite ground clause set \(G\) satisfy \[T_0\cup K\cup G\text{ is unsatisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_0\cup K[G]\cup G\text{ is unsatisfiable},\] where the right-hand problem includes the prescribed purification and congruence constraints. If this equivalence fails for some \(G\), then the reduction using that selected set \(K[G]\) is not complete for the extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locality guarantees completeness of the prescribed finite-instantiation reduction; a ground problem violating the locality equivalence witnesses incompleteness of that reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(T_1=T_0\cup K\) is a theory extension.
\(G\) ranges over finite ground clause sets.
\(K[G]\) is determined by a fixed ground-instance selection rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the displayed equivalence fails for some \(G\), the reduction based on \(K[G]\) is incomplete.

notation.meaning: Ground instances selected from the extension axioms for the problem G

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a combination procedure for theories \(T_1\) and \(T_2\).
\(G\) is a finite ground formula over the combined signature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Soundness means \(C(G)=\mathsf{SAT}\Rightarrow T_1\cup T_2\cup\{G\}\) is satisfiable and \(C(G)=\mathsf{UNSAT}\Rightarrow T_1\cup T_2\models\neg G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic soundness criterion for satisfiability answers from a theory-combination procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The procedure \(C\) is sound if every returned answer is semantically valid: \(C(G)=\mathsf{SAT}\) implies that some \((\Sigma_1\cup\Sigma_2)\)-structure satisfies \(T_1\cup T_2\cup\{G\}\), while \(C(G)=\mathsf{UNSAT}\) implies \(T_1\cup T_2\models\neg G\). Thus no compatible arrangement accepted by the component solvers may lack a combined model, and every learned conflict must be a consequence of the combined theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound combination procedure never reports satisfiable without a combined model and never reports unsatisfiable without a valid combined-theory conflict.
knowledge_statements.title: Combination Soundness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided semantic soundness criterion is mathematically coherent and the property kind fits the container, but no source or locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(T_1,T_2\) are stably infinite theories with disjoint nonlogical signatures, sharing equality and sorts only.
Ground satisfiability in each component theory is decidable.
All equality arrangements on shared purified constants are considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The arrangement-based combination procedure decides ground satisfiability in \(T_1\cup T_2\).

notation.meaning: A complete equality and disequality arrangement on shared constants

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nelson–Oppen completeness with exhaustive equality arrangements, avoiding a convexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite ground formula and let purification produce component constraints \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) with shared constants \(V\). Then \(T_1\cup T_2\cup\{G\}\) is satisfiable if and only if there exists a complete equality arrangement \(\alpha\) on \(V\) such that both \(T_1\cup G_1\cup\alpha\) and \(T_2\cup G_2\cup\alpha\) are satisfiable. Consequently, enumerating arrangements and invoking the component procedures is complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For disjoint stably infinite theories, exhaustive exchange of equality arrangements makes component satisfiability sufficient and necessary for combined satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Combination Completeness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exhaustive-arrangement theorem is a standard Nelson–Oppen completeness form, but it needs an authoritative locator confirming the many-sorted stable-infiniteness hypotheses and exact signature conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined-Model Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union construction for disjoint component signatures after aligning shared carriers and interface constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M_1\models T_1\cup G_1\cup\alpha\) and \(\mathcal M_2\models T_2\cup G_2\cup\alpha\). Suppose their shared-sort carriers are identical and their interpretations of every shared purified constant agree. Define a structure \(\mathcal M\) on those carriers by taking the interpretation of each private symbol in \(\Sigma_i\) from \(\mathcal M_i\). Then \(\mathcal M\upharpoonright_{\Sigma_i}=\mathcal M_i\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\), and \(\mathcal M\models T_1\cup T_2\cup G_1\cup G_2\cup\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once the shared carriers and interface constants are aligned, combining the private-symbol interpretations of the component models yields a model of both components.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M_i\models T_i\cup G_i\cup\alpha\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\).
\(\Sigma_1\) and \(\Sigma_2\) are disjoint outside equality, shared sorts, and purified interface constants.
The component models have identical shared-sort carriers and agree on all shared purified constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The union structure \(\mathcal M\) satisfies \(T_1\cup T_2\cup G_1\cup G_2\cup\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Structure formed by uniting their private-symbol interpretations
Common equality arrangement on purified interface constants

assumptions_latex: The theories share a nonempty sort \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate satisfiability does not imply combined satisfiability when the components impose incompatible finite cardinalities on a shared sort.

notation.meaning: Sentence asserting exactly n elements in sort s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal cardinality-spectrum obstruction on one shared sort.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1=\{\operatorname{Card}_s(1)\}\) and \(T_2=\{\operatorname{Card}_s(2)\}\), where \(\operatorname{Card}_s(n)\) states that sort \(s\) has exactly \(n\) elements. Each theory has a finite model. However, any model of \(T_1\cup T_2\) would have to satisfy both \(|s|=1\) and \(|s|=2\), which is impossible. Thus a combination method that exchanges only equalities and ignores shared-sort cardinality is incomplete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two separately satisfiable components requiring one and two elements in the same shared sort have no combined model.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Cardinality Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically valid and counterexample is the correct kind for this failure leaf, but no supporting citation or locator is provided.

assumptions_latex: The component signatures share a unary function symbol \(f:s\to s\).
Sort \(s\) may contain at least two elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The components are separately satisfiable but their union is inconsistent because the shared symbol \(f\) cannot receive both interpretations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct interference caused by incompatible axioms for a shared function symbol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1=\{\forall x:s,\ f(x)=x\}\) and \(T_2=\{\exists x:s,\ f(x)\neq x\}\). Theory \(T_1\) is satisfiable by interpreting \(f\) as the identity, and \(T_2\) is satisfiable on a two-element carrier by interpreting \(f\) nontrivially. Their union is unsatisfiable. Treating \(f\) as two private symbols would incorrectly erase this conflict, so disjoint-signature combination cannot be applied unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared-function axioms can be separately satisfiable yet mutually inconsistent, so treating the shared function as private is unsound.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Disjoint Signature Interference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shared-function counterexample is internally consistent and fits the failure container, but it lacks an inspectable source.

assumptions_latex: Purification yields shared constants \(a,b\).
One component entails \(a=b\), while the other contains \(a\neq b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A combination procedure that does not communicate the entailed equality \(a=b\) may accept both component states although their conjunction is inconsistent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness failure from omitting a necessary equality consequence at the solver interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(T_1\cup G_1\models a=b\) and \(G_2\) contains \(a\neq b\). The isolated calls may both return satisfiable because \(G_1\) does not explicitly contain \(a=b\) and \(T_2\cup G_2\) need not derive any further conflict. Nevertheless, \(T_1\cup T_2\cup G_1\cup G_2\) is unsatisfiable. Completeness therefore requires communicating the equality or exploring an arrangement that includes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one solver’s implied equality is not communicated to another solver holding the opposite disequality, the combination can miss an inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Interface Exchange

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The omitted-equality scenario correctly illustrates a completeness failure, but the relevant communication or arrangement protocol must be tied to an authoritative theory-combination source.

assumptions_latex: The first component is real closed field arithmetic.
The second component specifies the integers with additive order inside the real domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adding real multiplication to an integer predicate permits Diophantine encoding, so satisfiability in the combined theory is undecidable although the component theories are decidable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical undecidability mechanism from combining real multiplication with an integer predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the combined structure \((\mathbb R,0,1,+,\times,<,Z)\), where \(Z(x)\) holds exactly for integer-valued reals, every Diophantine instance has the form \[\exists x_1\cdots x_n\;\bigl(Z(x_1)\land\cdots\land Z(x_n)\land p(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\bigr).\] Deciding these sentences would decide whether arbitrary integer polynomials have integer zeros. Hence the combination of decidable real closed field arithmetic with a decidable additive integer interface need not remain decidable once their symbols jointly express integer multiplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combining real multiplication with an integer predicate encodes arbitrary Diophantine equations, destroying decidability despite decidable components.
knowledge_statements.title: Undecidable Combined Theories

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Diophantine encoding is plausible, but the exact theories and signatures of the two individually decidable components are not formally specified or cited. A precise source is necessary before asserting that this structure arises as their undecidable combination.

children.title: Quantified SMT Extension Family
children.top_down_role: Cross-theory methods for quantified formulas, finite models, elimination, and axiomatized extensions; separated from quantifier-free theory families.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Decision Procedures: An Algorithmic Point of View
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Quantified formulas and decidable fragments
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Decision Procedures: An Algorithmic Point of View

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Quantifier reasoning in SMT

children.title: Quantifier Trigger Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection and quality regimes for patterns attached to quantified formulas.

knowledge_statements.title: Quantifier Trigger Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility conditions for user- or solver-selected triggers in E-matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a quantified formula \(Q=\forall \bar{x}\,\varphi(\bar{x})\), a finite trigger family \(T=\{P_1,\ldots,P_r\}\) is admissible when every \(P_i\) is a nonvariable term occurring in \(\varphi\), every variable in \(\bar{x}\) occurs in at least one \(P_i\), and no \(P_i\) contains a variable outside \(\bar{x}\). A selection policy ranks admissible families and returns one minimizing its implementation-specific cost, such as estimated match count or term generality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trigger is admissible when its patterns come from the quantified body, collectively cover all quantified variables, and introduce no additional variables.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=\forall\bar{x}\,\varphi(\bar{x})\) is a first-order quantified formula.
Candidate trigger terms are drawn from subterms of \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ admissible}\iff (\forall i\;P_i\in\operatorname{Sub}(\varphi))\land\operatorname{Var}(T)=\{\bar{x}\}\land(\forall i\;P_i\notin\operatorname{Var})\).

notation.meaning: terms occurring in the quantified body
variables occurring across all trigger patterns

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: common admissibility convention for SMT E-matching triggers
source_gap: supplied source locators do not concern quantified SMT

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the asserted admissibility convention or the claim that selection minimizes an implementation-specific cost. “Trigger family” should also be distinguished explicitly from one conjunctive multipattern versus a set of alternative multipatterns.

children.title: E-Matching Instantiation
children.top_down_role: Instantiation driven by matching trigger patterns against congruence-class terms.

knowledge_statements.title: E-Matching Instantiation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Congruence-aware matching of triggers against the current ground-term database.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a quantified formula \(\forall\bar{x}\,\varphi(\bar{x})\), trigger family \(T\), ground terms \(G\), and congruence relation \(\equiv_E\) maintained by the SMT solver. Enumerate substitutions \(\sigma\) mapping every variable in \(\bar{x}\) to ground terms such that, for each trigger pattern \(P\in T\), some \(g\in G\) satisfies \(P\sigma\equiv_E g\). For every previously unprocessed substitution, add the ground instance \(\varphi\sigma\); stop when no new match is available or a resource limit is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: E-matching finds ground substitutions whose trigger instances are congruent to known terms and adds the corresponding quantified-body instances.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is closed under the ground terms currently registered by the solver.
\(\equiv_E\) is a congruence relation on registered ground terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\varphi\sigma: \forall P\in T\;\exists g\in G,\ P\sigma\equiv_E g\}\) is the generated instance set.
review_flags: source_gap: an authoritative SMT quantifier-reasoning locator is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the precise congruence-aware matching and stopping semantics. The meaning of T also depends on whether it denotes one multipattern or alternative triggers.

children.title: Multipattern Trigger Regimes
children.top_down_role: Trigger configurations requiring coordinated matches across multiple patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Multipattern Trigger Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjunctive matching semantics for triggers composed of several patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=\{P_1,\ldots,P_k\}\) be one multipattern for \(\forall\bar{x}\,\varphi\). A substitution \(\sigma\) activates \(T\) exactly when every \(P_i\) matches a registered ground term modulo the same congruence relation and the matches agree on every shared variable: \[\operatorname{Active}(T,\sigma)\iff\bigwedge_{i=1}^{k}\exists g_i\in G\;(P_i\sigma\equiv_E g_i).\] Different multipatterns attached to the quantifier are alternatives, whereas patterns inside one multipattern are conjunctive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All patterns in one multipattern must match consistently under one substitution; distinct multipatterns provide alternative activation routes.
assumptions_latex: Every quantified variable occurs in at least one \(P_i\).
All component matches use the same ground-term database and congruence relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ generates }\varphi\sigma\iff\operatorname{Active}(T,\sigma)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard conjunctive interpretation of SMT multipatterns
source_gap: supplied locators provide no trigger-semantics evidence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role and conjunctive shared-substitution formulation fit the leaf, but the distinction between conjunctive component patterns and alternative multipatterns lacks cited support.

children.title: Trigger-Match Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Missed, excessive, or unstable matches arising from trigger choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Trigger-Match Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incompleteness caused by absence of a syntactic or congruence trigger match.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\forall x\,((f(x)=f(x))\land P(x))\) with selected trigger \(f(x)\), together with the ground assertion \(\neg P(a)\). The set is first-order inconsistent. If the registered ground database initially contains \(a\) but no term congruent to \(f(t)\) for any ground \(t\), E-matching produces no substitution for the quantifier. Thus trigger-only instantiation may fail to expose the conflicting instance \(P(a)\), despite semantic unsatisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semantically necessary instance can remain undiscovered when no registered ground term matches the selected trigger.
assumptions_latex: Instantiation is performed solely by E-matching the selected trigger.
The initial database contains no ground term headed by \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\cap\{t:\operatorname{head}(t)=f\}=\varnothing\implies\operatorname{Matches}(f(x),G)=\varnothing\), although the formula set is unsatisfiable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit counterfamily demonstrates trigger incompleteness
source_gap: authoritative documentation of the operational boundary is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example plausibly demonstrates trigger-only incompleteness and the failure-boundary kind is appropriate, but the operational assumptions about registered terms and congruence matching require an authoritative SMT source.

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-Based Quantifier Instantiation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-guided generation of quantified instances that conflict with a candidate ground model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given ground constraints \(F\), a universal formula \(Q=\forall\bar{x}\,\varphi(\bar{x})\), and a candidate model \(M\models F\), solve the counterexample query \(M,\bar{x}\models\neg\varphi(\bar{x})\) under the theory-specific search procedure. If it yields values represented by ground terms \(\bar{t}\), add \(\varphi(\bar{t})\) to \(F\), retain the resulting conflict or propagation lemma, and repeat. If the query is certified unsatisfiable for every active quantifier, accept \(M\) with respect to those quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CBQI searches a candidate model for a violating tuple and adds the associated ground instance until no violation remains.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) satisfies the current ground abstraction \(F\).
Counterexample values can be represented by admissible ground terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\models\neg\varphi(\bar{t})\implies F\leftarrow F\land\varphi(\bar{t})\).

notation.meaning: ground representatives of a violating tuple

review_flags: source_gap: exact CBQI variants depend on the background theory and require a specific source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but this generic candidate-model counterexample loop risks conflating conflict-based quantifier instantiation with MBQI. The theory-specific conflict construction and the condition for accepting a model require a precise CBQI source.

children.title: Instantiation Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Prioritization and timing of candidate quantifier instantiations.

knowledge_statements.title: Instantiation Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Priority-based selection of pending quantified instances during SMT search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a queue \(C\) of candidate pairs \((Q,\sigma)\), a processed set \(H\), and a priority score \(s(Q,\sigma,S)\) depending on solver state \(S\). Repeatedly remove a minimum-score candidate not equivalent to an element of \(H\), add its ground instance to the solver, insert its canonical signature into \(H\), update \(S\) and candidate scores, and enqueue newly enabled matches. Stop at a conflict, a fixed point, or the current round's instantiation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scheduler prioritizes pending quantifier substitutions, emits unseen instances, and updates priorities as the solver state changes.
assumptions_latex: Candidate substitutions ground every variable of their quantifier.
The scoring rule induces a deterministic tie-breaking order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((Q,\sigma)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in C\setminus H}s(c,S)\) is instantiated at each scheduling step.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: abstract scheduling interface common to instantiation engines
source_gap: concrete fairness and priority policies vary across solvers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but no source supports this particular priority-queue scheduler. Moreover, C contains candidate pairs while H contains signatures, so C\setminus H and the displayed argmin are not well-typed without comparing candidate signatures against H.

children.title: Instantiation Redundancy Control
children.top_down_role: Detection or suppression of duplicate and subsumed instantiations.

knowledge_statements.title: Instantiation Redundancy Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical suppression of duplicate or congruence-equivalent ground instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a quantified formula \(Q\) and ground substitution \(\sigma\), define the instance signature \(\kappa(Q,\sigma)\) by canonically representing \(\varphi_Q\sigma\) modulo the solver's current congruence and chosen syntactic normalization. The candidate is redundant when its signature is already stored: \[\operatorname{Redundant}(Q,\sigma,H)\iff\kappa(Q,\sigma)\in H.\] A redundancy-controlled engine emits only nonredundant candidates and inserts each emitted signature into \(H\). This prevents exact or normalized duplicates without claiming logical-subsumption completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance is suppressed when its canonicalized ground formula has already been emitted under the selected normalization.
assumptions_latex: Canonicalization preserves equality modulo the solver's current congruence.
\(H\) contains every previously emitted canonical signature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(Q,\sigma)\in H\implies\varphi_Q\sigma\text{ is not emitted again}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical signature caching is a standard duplicate-control abstraction
source_gap: normalization strength and congruence handling are implementation-specific

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but congruence-aware canonicalization and duplicate suppression are implementation-specific and unsupported by a cited locator. A source must clarify whether canonical signatures remain valid as the solver congruence evolves.

children.title: Instantiation-Budget Regimes
children.top_down_role: Resource limits governing quantifier-instantiation effort.

knowledge_statements.title: Instantiation-Budget Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-round and global resource bounds for quantified-instance generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n_r\) be the number of instances emitted in solver round \(r\), \(c(I)\ge 0\) the charged cost of instance \(I\), and \(B_r,B_{\mathrm{tot}}\) fixed budgets. A run obeys the budget regime when \[n_r\le B_r\quad\text{for every }r,\qquad \sum_{I\text{ emitted}}c(I)\le B_{\mathrm{tot}}.\] Once either applicable bound is exhausted, further candidates are deferred or discarded according to the scheduling policy; consequently, finite budgets do not by themselves ensure quantifier completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Instantiation may be limited per round and globally; exhausting either budget postpones candidates and can sacrifice completeness.
assumptions_latex: Every emitted instance has a nonnegative charged cost.
Budget counters are monotone during their respective accounting intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n_r=B_r\lor\sum_I c(I)=B_{\mathrm{tot}}\implies\text{no further charged emission in the applicable interval}\).

notation.meaning: cost charged to an emitted instance

review_flags: source_gap: no supplied source documents quantified-instantiation budgets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the combined per-round count and global charged-cost regime is an invented abstraction without cited solver documentation. The boundary conclusion also assumes emissions cannot have zero charged cost after total-cost exhaustion.

children.title: Scheduling–Redundancy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions among candidate priority, duplication cost, plus search progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling–Redundancy Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational tradeoff between early duplicate filtering and scheduling cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a multiset of candidate instances, \(U=\{\kappa(I):I\in C\}\) its distinct canonical signatures, and \(b\) an emission budget. Canonical filtering before scheduling restricts expensive ranking to \(U\) and prevents duplicate emissions, but computing \(\kappa\) for every candidate incurs preprocessing cost. Scheduling before full canonicalization may reduce immediate preprocessing, yet duplicate candidates can consume queue capacity or budget. Thus the preferred order depends on canonicalization cost, duplicate multiplicity, and the budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Early deduplication saves ranking and emission work when duplicates are common, but its canonicalization cost may outweigh those savings.
assumptions_latex: Emitting two candidates with the same signature yields no additional retained instance.
Canonicalization and priority evaluation have nonnegative costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{early filtering ranks }|U|\text{ items, whereas unfiltered scheduling may rank }|C|\text{ items, with }|U|\le |C|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cost tradeoff follows from explicit candidate and signature counts
source_gap: solver-specific cost models and empirical thresholds need evidence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits, but the operational cost comparison is unsupported and depends on solver-specific queue and canonicalization behavior. The emission budget b is introduced but does not participate in the formal conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Based Quantifier Instantiation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate-model validation by searching for falsifying quantified assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a ground abstraction \(F\), universal formulas \(Q_j=\forall\bar{x}_j\,\varphi_j\), and a candidate model \(M\models F\). For each \(Q_j\), search for \(\bar{a}\) such that \(M\models\neg\varphi_j(\bar{a})\). If found, choose ground representatives \(\bar{t}\) interpreted as \(\bar{a}\) and add \(\varphi_j(\bar{t})\) to \(F\). Recompute the ground model and repeat. Return satisfiable only when every quantified body holds for all assignments in the model domain, subject to the completeness guarantees of the background fragment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MBQI tests quantified formulas in a candidate model and adds ground instances for assignments that falsify their bodies.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) satisfies the current ground abstraction.
Violating model values admit usable ground representatives or equivalent instantiation terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\models\neg\varphi_j(\bar{a})\implies F\leftarrow F\land\varphi_j(\bar{t})\), where \(M(\bar{t})=\bar{a}\).
review_flags: source_gap: fragment-dependent completeness conditions require an authoritative MBQI source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but ground representability of model values, counterexample search, and the final satisfiability condition vary by MBQI implementation and logical fragment. An authoritative source with exact completeness conditions is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Model Finding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-domain search for models of quantified first-order constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each uninterpreted sort \(S\), choose a finite cardinality bound \(k_S\ge 1\) and introduce representatives \(d^S_1,\ldots,d^S_{k_S}\). Encode constants, function tables, predicates, ground constraints, and every quantified formula over these finite domains; universal quantifiers expand over all representative tuples and existential quantifiers over finite disjunctions. Solve the resulting finite constraint problem. A satisfying table interpretation yields a finite model; if unsatisfiable, enlarge selected bounds and repeat, unless an independent argument proves that no larger model is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-model finding bounds each sort, encodes functions and quantifiers over finite representatives, and enlarges bounds when necessary.
assumptions_latex: All selected sort bounds are positive finite integers.
Function and predicate interpretations are encoded over the complete bounded domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SAT}(E_{\mathbf{k}})\implies\text{the original formula has a model with }|S|\le k_S\text{ for every bounded sort }S\).

notation.meaning: finite-domain encoding at the selected bounds

review_flags: source_gap: completeness and symmetry-breaking variants require a finite-model-finding source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but the encoding and bound-enlargement procedure lack a finite-model-finding source. It must also be clarified whether the representatives are constrained distinct, since that determines whether k_S is an exact cardinality or merely an upper bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Quantified Model Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic certificate for a candidate model satisfying quantified formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) provide a nonempty domain \(D_S\) for every sort, interpretations of all constants and functions with the declared types, and truth relations for predicates. For each asserted quantified formula, evaluate its body using these interpretations and the corresponding variable assignments. The structure \(M\) is a quantified-model certificate precisely when it satisfies every ground assertion and \[M\models\forall\bar{x}\,\varphi\iff\text{for every }\bar{a}\in D_{ar{x}},\ M[\bar{x}\mapsto\bar{a}]\models\varphi.\] For finite domains, exhaustive evaluation makes this certificate directly checkable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantified model supplies typed domains and symbol interpretations and satisfies each quantified body under every domain assignment.
assumptions_latex: Every sort domain in \(M\) is nonempty.
All symbol interpretations are total and respect their declared sorts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\models F\iff M\text{ satisfies every ground assertion and every quantified assertion in }F\).

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of domains for the variables in the tuple

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard many-sorted first-order satisfaction criterion
source_gap: supplied source inventory contains no quantified-model semantics locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits, but no source supports the stated semantic certificate. The display contains malformed notation D_{ar{x}} instead of D_{\bar{x}}, and direct finite-domain checkability presupposes effectively represented interpretations and decidable evaluation of the bodies.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Quantifier Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination relative to a fixed first-order arithmetic theory and formula class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a first-order arithmetic theory and let \(\mathcal C\) be a class of formulas closed under substitution. Quantifier elimination for \(T\) on \(\mathcal C\) is an effective map \(\operatorname{QE}_T\) such that, for every \(\varphi(\bar x)\in\mathcal C\), the formula \(\operatorname{QE}_T(\varphi)(\bar x)\) is quantifier-free and \[T\models \forall\bar x\,\bigl(\varphi(\bar x)\leftrightarrow \operatorname{QE}_T(\varphi)(\bar x)\bigr).\] For elimination of variables \(\bar y\), this applies to \(\varphi(\bar x)=Q\bar y\,\theta(\bar x,\bar y)\), where \(Q\bar y\) is the specified quantifier prefix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quantifier elimination effectively replaces each supported arithmetic formula by a quantifier-free formula equivalent in the chosen theory.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and the supported formula class \(\mathcal C\) are fixed.
\(\operatorname{QE}_T\) terminates on every input in \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\models\varphi\leftrightarrow\operatorname{QE}_T(\varphi)\), with \(\operatorname{QE}_T(\varphi)\) quantifier-free.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard semantic definition of effective quantifier elimination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable authoritative source is cited for the stated effective, class-relative formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Based Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-image, model-indexed projection for existential theory formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a theory, let \(\lambda(\bar x,\bar y)\) be quantifier-free, and let \(M\models_T\lambda\). A model-based projection operator returns a quantifier-free formula \(\pi(M,\lambda)(\bar x)\) satisfying \[M\models\pi(M,\lambda),\qquad T\models\forall\bar x\bigl(\pi(M,\lambda)(\bar x)\rightarrow\exists\bar y\,\lambda(\bar x,\bar y)\bigr).\] It has finite image for \(\lambda\) when the set \(\{\pi(M,\lambda):M\models_T\lambda\}\) is finite modulo \(T\)-equivalence. If its outputs also cover every model of \(\exists\bar y\,\lambda\), their finite disjunction is a quantifier-free elimination result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model-based projection produces a model-satisfied sufficient condition for an existential formula; a finite covering image yields quantifier elimination.
assumptions_latex: \(M\models_T\lambda(\bar x,\bar y)\).
The projection output contains only the free variables \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\models\pi(M,\lambda)\) and \(T\models\pi(M,\lambda)\rightarrow\exists\bar y\,\lambda\).

notation.meaning: a theory model satisfying the input formula

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-image model-based projection specification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The specification resembles finite-image model-based projection, but an authoritative source is needed to confirm the precise model/assignment semantics and covering condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Specific Elimination Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract contract between a quantified SMT engine and a theory eliminator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed theory \(T\), the interface accepts a quantifier-free formula \(\lambda(\bar x,\bar y)\), an elimination set \(\bar y\), and optionally a model \(M\models_T\lambda\). It returns either a quantifier-free formula \(\psi(\bar x)\), a finite family \(\Psi\), or \(\mathsf{unsupported}\). An exact result must satisfy \[T\models\forall\bar x\bigl(\psi(\bar x)\leftrightarrow\exists\bar y\,\lambda(\bar x,\bar y)\bigr).\] A projected family must satisfy \(T\models\chi\rightarrow\exists\bar y\,\lambda\) for every \(\chi\in\Psi\), and it may be marked complete only when \[T\models\forall\bar x\bigl((\exists\bar y\,\lambda(\bar x,\bar y))\rightarrow\bigvee_{\chi\in\Psi}\chi(\bar x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A theory-elimination interface represents successful results as an exact elimination or a family of sound projected cases, and otherwise reports unsupported; every completeness claim carries an explicit coverage obligation.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) fixes the semantics of all theory symbols in \(\lambda\).
\(\bar x\cap\bar y=\varnothing\).
Every \(\chi\in\Psi\) has free variables only from \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every successful response is theory-sound, and every response marked complete covers \(\exists\bar y\,\lambda\).

notation.meaning: interface response making no elimination claim

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: semantic interface contract synthesized from exact and model-based elimination obligations

knowledge_statements.title: Local Theory Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ground locality for an extension of a base theory by axioms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_0\) be a base theory and let \(T_1=T_0\cup K\), where \(K\) contains axioms over additional function symbols. The extension is local when, for every finite set \(G\) of ground clauses, \[T_1\cup G\text{ is unsatisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_0\cup K[G]\cup G\text{ is unsatisfiable},\] where \(K[G]\) is the finite set of ground instances of \(K\) whose extension-headed ground terms are drawn from the extension terms occurring in \(G\) or in the relevant axioms. Thus ground satisfiability in the extension reduces to finitely many instances plus a base-theory check.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A theory extension is local when every finite ground problem is decided using only axiom instances built from extension terms already present in that problem.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite set of ground clauses.
\(K[G]\) is finite under the stated term restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_0\cup K\cup G\) is unsatisfiable exactly when \(T_0\cup K[G]\cup G\) is unsatisfiable.

notation.meaning: local finite set of ground axiom instances

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard ground-locality characterization of local theory extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has the right definitional role, but locality conventions differ in the precise construction of \(K[G]\). A source is required to verify the stated term restriction.

knowledge_statements.title: Axiom-Instantiation Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic trigger- or term-driven instantiation loop for quantified extension axioms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite ground clause set \(G\), universally quantified axioms \(K\), and a base-theory decision procedure. Initialize \(S:=G\). Repeatedly select \(\forall\bar x\,A(\bar x)\in K\) and a ground substitution \(\sigma\) licensed by the framework's trigger or term policy, then set \(S:=S\cup\{A\sigma\}\). Stop with \(\mathsf{unsat}\) when the ground solver refutes \(S\). Stop with \(\mathsf{sat}\) at a fixed point only if the selected fragment guarantees completeness of the generated instances; otherwise return \(\mathsf{unknown}\) at a fixed point or resource limit. Duplicate instances do not change \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The framework repeatedly adds policy-selected ground axiom instances and invokes a ground solver, reporting satisfiable only when a completeness condition justifies the fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and ground.
The base-theory procedure is sound for every generated ground set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reported \(\mathsf{unsat}\) is sound; a reported \(\mathsf{sat}\) requires a complete fixed-point criterion.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard saturation-style quantified-axiom instantiation loop

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits, and the outcome discipline is cautious, but the generic trigger policy and complete fixed-point criterion require a specific instantiation-framework source.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Extension Combination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient modular combination principle for compatible extensions of a shared base theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1=T_0\cup K_1\) and \(T_2=T_0\cup K_2\) have extension signatures disjoint outside the shared base signature. Suppose each finite ground problem can be reduced completely to finitely many purified instances over \(T_0\), and the component procedures exchange all required equalities and disequalities among shared constants. Then a combined ground set \(G\) is satisfiable in \(T_1\cup T_2\) exactly when there exists a consistent arrangement of the shared constants for which both purified component reductions are satisfiable over compatible \(T_0\)-models. Failure of signature, model-compatibility, or completeness assumptions invalidates this equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible local extensions can be combined through purification and shared equalities when their signatures, base models, and component reductions satisfy the required modularity conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma_1\cap\Sigma_2=\Sigma_0\) outside logical symbols.
Each component reduction is finite, sound, and complete for ground inputs.
The component base models can be amalgamated under each accepted shared arrangement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is satisfiable in \(T_1\cup T_2\) iff some shared arrangement makes both purified component problems compatibly satisfiable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The modular combination claim is source-sensitive: purification, arrangements, model compatibility, and amalgamation require an exact theorem and hypotheses before the stated equivalence is reliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Instantiation Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite trigger-generated term growth from one satisfiable quantified axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the satisfiable set \[G=\{P(a),\ \forall x\,(P(x)\rightarrow P(f(x)))\}.\] If the quantified axiom uses trigger \(P(x)\), matching \(P(a)\) produces \(P(f(a))\); matching that term produces \(P(f^2(a))\), and inductively the procedure generates \(P(f^n(a))\) for every \(n\ge 0\). No finite stage is a trigger fixed point, although \(G\) has a model, for example one interpreting \(P\) as the whole domain. Hence unrestricted trigger saturation need not terminate even on a satisfiable input containing one universal axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trigger on P(x) repeatedly creates P(f(x)), producing infinitely many terms even though the quantified input is satisfiable.
assumptions_latex: The instantiation policy eagerly processes every newly matched trigger term.
Distinct terms \(f^n(a)\) are not identified by ground reasoning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated instance sequence is infinite, so the saturation procedure does not reach a finite fixed point.

notation.meaning: n-fold application of f to a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally coherent and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but it has no inspectable citation supporting its use as a canonical instantiation-divergence example.

children.title: Trigger Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Solver behavior changes caused by trigger selection or pattern availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Trigger Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of generated instances on syntactically different trigger selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an axiom set \(K\), ground context \(G\), and trigger selection \(\tau\), let \(\operatorname{Cl}_{\tau}(G,K)\) be the least ground set closed under all matches licensed by \(\tau\). Trigger sensitivity occurs when two admissible selections \(\tau_1,\tau_2\) satisfy \[\operatorname{Cl}_{\tau_1}(G,K)\not\equiv_T\operatorname{Cl}_{\tau_2}(G,K),\] or when one closure is finite and the other is infinite. For \(K=\{\forall x(P(x)\rightarrow P(f(x)))\}\) and \(G=\{P(a)\}\), trigger \(P(x)\) generates an infinite chain, whereas trigger \(P(f(x))\) initially has no match. Thus termination and deductive progress are not invariant under trigger choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two legal triggers for the same quantified problem may generate different closures, including finite versus infinite behavior or unequal deductive strength.
assumptions_latex: Trigger matching is syntactic modulo the solver's stated matching theory.
Only trigger-licensed substitutions are generated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Instantiation progress or termination can change when \(\tau_1\) is replaced by \(\tau_2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalized operational notion of trigger sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example plausibly demonstrates trigger sensitivity, but admissible-trigger and closure semantics are solver-framework dependent and need a canonical source.

children.title: Model Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Quantifier-reasoning behavior changes caused by candidate-model structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Model Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-guided instantiation dependence on the ground solver's choice among candidate models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a ground context and \(Q=\forall\bar x\,A(\bar x)\). A model-guided instantiator is model-sensitive at \((G,Q)\) if there exist models \(M_1,M_2\models_TG\) for which its selected substitution sets differ: \[I(M_1,G,Q)\ne I(M_2,G,Q).\] The sensitivity is semantically consequential when the resulting instances are not equivalent relative to \(T\cup G\), or operationally consequential when their generated search trees have different finiteness behavior. Consequently, unless the selection rule is invariant or fair over candidate models, changing only the ground model may alter progress, termination, or discovery of a refuting instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model sensitivity holds when different candidate models of the same ground context cause model-guided quantifier reasoning to select materially different instances.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1,M_2\models_TG\).
The instantiator may inspect interpretations supplied by the current model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(M_1,G,Q)\ne I(M_2,G,Q)\), with potentially inequivalent search consequences.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational condition for dependence on candidate-model choice

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but the meanings of candidate model, selected substitution set, and semantic consequence depend on a particular model-guided instantiation calculus.

children.title: Trigger-Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Input regimes where small trigger changes produce materially different instantiation behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Trigger-Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-closure boundary ensuring termination of trigger instantiation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix quantified axioms \(K\), a ground context \(G\), and triggers \(\tau\). Let \(U\) be a finite set of ground terms containing every ground term of \(G\). The triple \((G,K,\tau)\) is trigger-stable over \(U\) when every substitution obtained by matching a trigger against terms in \(U\) produces an axiom instance whose ground subterms also lie in \(U\). Under duplicate elimination and exhaustive matching, no terms outside \(U\) can then arise, so only finitely many trigger substitutions and ground instances are possible. If no such finite closed \(U\) exists, this termination argument does not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trigger stability is guaranteed by a finite term universe closed under every trigger-generated instance; outside that boundary, finite saturation is not ensured.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and contains all ground terms initially occurring in \(G\).
Matching over \(U\) has finitely many substitutions and duplicate instances are discarded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Trigger saturation terminates after finitely many distinct instances whenever \(U\) is closed under trigger generation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-state closure condition directly implies termination

children.title: Model-Guidance Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Candidate-model features that misdirect, delay, or destabilize quantified reasoning.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Guidance Failure Modes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of completeness when model-guided selection lacks fairness over persistent violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M_n)_{n\ge0}\) be candidate models produced during search and let \(V(M_n,Q)\) be the set of ground substitutions witnessing violations of a quantified formula \(Q\). A model-guidance failure occurs if there is a substitution \(\sigma^\ast\) that remains necessary for a refutation, yet the selection rule chooses \(S_n\subseteq V(M_n,Q)\) with \(\sigma^\ast\notin\bigcup_{n\ge0}S_n\). The procedure may then generate infinitely many irrelevant or redundant instances, oscillate among candidate models, or reach an unjustified apparent fixed point. Completeness therefore requires a fairness or finite-cover property ensuring that every persistent relevant violation is eventually selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model guidance can miss a necessary instance forever unless its selection policy fairly covers persistent quantified violations.
assumptions_latex: \(\sigma^\ast\) is required by every finite refutation available to the instantiation calculus.
The selection policy is not fair with respect to persistent violations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure to select \(\sigma^\ast\) prevents the calculus from guaranteeing discovery of the refutation.

notation.meaning: violating substitutions exposed by the model

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fairness boundary for model-guided instantiation completeness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon fits the leaf, but necessity of a substitution and the fairness condition are calculus-relative; a published model-guidance result is needed to validate the completeness claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Quantified Fragments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Calculus-relative incompleteness for a syntactically specified quantified fragment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of quantified formulas over a theory \(T\), and let \(\mathcal C\) be a sound proof-search calculus whose accepted outcomes are \(T\)-satisfiability certificates and \(T\)-refutations. The fragment \(\mathcal F\) is incomplete for \(\mathcal C\) when there exists \(\varphi\in\mathcal F\) such that either \(T\cup\{\varphi\}\) is satisfiable but \(\mathcal C\) cannot derive an accepted satisfiability certificate, or \(T\cup\{\varphi\}\) is unsatisfiable but \(\mathcal C\) cannot derive a refutation. Operationally, a fair run on such an input may diverge or return \(\mathsf{unknown}\). This is distinct from undecidability of the fragment because incompleteness may belong to the chosen calculus even when another terminating decision procedure exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantified fragment is incomplete for a calculus when some formula in the fragment has a definite satisfiability status relative to the theory but the calculus cannot certify that status.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is sound for every accepted satisfiability certificate and refutation.
\(\mathcal F\) and the background theory \(T\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\varphi\in\mathcal F\) whose correct satisfiability status relative to \(T\) cannot be established by \(\mathcal C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: calculus-relative definition of incompleteness with satisfiability distinguished from validity

knowledge_statements.title: Undecidable Quantified Theories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical undecidability boundary for unrestricted first-order quantification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a first-order language with equality and at least one binary relation symbol. The set \(\operatorname{Val}(L)\) of logically valid \(L\)-sentences is undecidable. Consequently, no algorithm can, for every quantified \(L\)-sentence \(\varphi\), terminate and correctly decide whether \(\varphi\) is valid. Equivalently, no quantified-SMT procedure for this unrestricted class can simultaneously be sound, complete, and terminating on every input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unrestricted first-order validity is undecidable, so no quantified solver can be sound, complete, and terminating on all such formulas.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a first-order language with equality and a binary relation symbol.
Inputs permit unrestricted first-order quantifier alternation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Val}(L)\) is undecidable; hence no total sound-and-complete decision procedure exists for the class.

notation.meaning: Set of logically valid sentences of the language L.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and statement fit the node, but the exact signature threshold for undecidability is a nontrivial theorem requiring an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: SMT Assurance-Complexity Landscape
children.top_down_role: Guarantee families for DPLL(T), learned theory information, model generation, proof artifacts, trust boundaries, and fragment complexity.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Correctness, models, proofs, unsatisfiable cores, and interpolants
SMT proof systems and complexity

knowledge_statements.title: DPLL(T) Soundness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness of quantifier-free DPLL(T) answers under valid theory information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a quantifier-free formula over theory \(T\). Assume every learned theory clause \(L\) satisfies \(T\models L\), every reported theory conflict is genuinely \(T\)-inconsistent, and every reported model satisfies both \(T\) and \(F\). If DPLL(T) returns \(\mathsf{unsat}\), its Boolean abstraction together with the learned theory clauses is propositionally inconsistent, which implies \(T\models\neg F\). If it returns \(\mathsf{sat}\) with interpretation \(\mathcal M\), then \(\mathcal M\models T\land F\). Thus either definitive answer is correct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid theory lemmas, sound conflicts, and checked models ensure that every SAT or UNSAT answer produced by DPLL(T) is correct.
assumptions_latex: Every learned theory lemma is \(T\)-valid.
Theory conflicts and propagations are sound.
A returned model is checked against \(T\land F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A returned \(\mathsf{sat}\) or \(\mathsf{unsat}\) answer is semantically correct for \(F\) modulo \(T\).

notation.meaning: Interpretation returned with a satisfiable result.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property matches DPLL(T) soundness and states appropriate semantic conditions, but no cited source supports the soundness implication or the assumed theory-information interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: DPLL(T) Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Refutational and model completeness for a finite quantifier-free DPLL(T) search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be quantifier-free with finitely many theory atoms. Suppose satisfiability of finite conjunctions of \(T\)-literals is decidable by a terminating complete theory solver. If the Boolean search is fair, every theory-inconsistent total assignment yields a valid blocking clause, and the procedure does not revisit a blocked total assignment, then DPLL(T) terminates. It returns \(\mathsf{sat}\) exactly when some Boolean assignment for \(F\) is extendable to a \(T\)-model, and otherwise returns \(\mathsf{unsat}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finite atoms, a complete terminating theory solver, fair search, and permanent conflict blocking, DPLL(T) decides quantifier-free satisfiability modulo T.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has finitely many theory atoms.
The theory solver decides finite conjunctions of \(T\)-literals.
Boolean search is fair and theory-conflicting assignments are permanently blocked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DPLL(T) terminates and returns \(\mathsf{sat}\iff F\) is satisfiable modulo \(T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and finite-search hypotheses are plausible, but completeness and termination depend on the precise DPLL(T) calculus and require an authoritative source with a theorem or section locator.

children.title: DPLL(T) Fairness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search and theory-processing schedules relevant to eventual exploration obligations.

knowledge_statements.title: DPLL(T) Fairness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational fairness condition preventing persistent DPLL(T) work from being starved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DPLL(T) run is fair if every inference or search obligation that remains continuously enabled is eventually selected. In particular, each unblocked relevant Boolean assignment is eventually explored or excluded by learning, each pending theory-consistency check is eventually performed, and restarts do not indefinitely postpone a persistent decision or propagation. A weaker assignment-fair regime requires only eventual exploration or exclusion of every relevant total Boolean assignment; an inference-fair regime additionally covers persistent propagation and theory-check obligations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fair DPLL(T) scheduler eventually handles every persistent assignment, propagation, and theory-check obligation instead of starving it through choices or restarts.
assumptions_latex: The run has a specified set of relevant Boolean assignments and enabled inference obligations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fairness holds exactly when no continuously enabled required obligation is postponed forever.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the fairness-regimes leaf, but fairness obligations vary by calculus and scheduler. A source defining the applicable DPLL(T) fairness regime is required.

children.title: DPLL(T) Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fragments plus architectural conditions supporting terminating solver runs.

knowledge_statements.title: DPLL(T) Termination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient termination regime for finite-atom DPLL(T).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the input contain \(n<\infty\) distinct theory atoms, and suppose every theory call terminates. A DPLL(T) run is in a finite-progress termination regime when each conflict learns a clause not already entailed by the current learned-clause database, learned blocking clauses are retained, and restarts preserve them. Since only finitely many Boolean clauses over \(n\) atoms exist, only finitely many strict learning steps can occur; between such steps, terminating Boolean search explores a finite space. Therefore the complete run terminates with a definitive result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite atoms, terminating theory calls, retained nonredundant learning, and finite Boolean search suffice to make DPLL(T) terminate.
assumptions_latex: The input has \(n<\infty\) theory atoms.
Every theory call and each Boolean-search phase terminates.
Each conflict produces a retained clause that gives strict progress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The DPLL(T) run performs finitely many learning phases and terminates.

notation.meaning: Number of distinct theory atoms in the input.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition gives a coherent finite-progress regime, but the termination argument depends on retained strict learning and terminating search phases; these calculus-specific assumptions need authoritative support.

children.title: Fairness–Termination Dependence
children.top_down_role: Structural dependence of termination guarantees on fair search or theory scheduling.

knowledge_statements.title: Fairness–Termination Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation and joint role of fairness and progress in DPLL(T) completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fairness and termination are distinct properties of a DPLL(T) run. Termination alone does not imply completeness, because a terminating scheduler may omit a relevant assignment or theory check. Fairness alone does not imply termination, because a fair run may generate infinitely many distinct obligations. For a finite-atom calculus with terminating theory calls and retained strict-progress learning, fairness prevents starvation while finiteness prevents infinite progress; together they yield termination after exhaustive coverage and hence support completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fairness prevents starvation, while finite strict progress prevents infinite execution; neither property alone generally supplies complete terminating search.
assumptions_latex: The completeness claim concerns a finite-atom DPLL(T) calculus.
Theory calls terminate and learned progress is retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fairness plus finite strict progress supports complete termination, whereas neither condition implies the other in general.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle appropriately separates fairness from termination, but its joint completeness claim is calculus-dependent and lacks a supporting source with a specific locator.

children.title: Nontermination Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Solver regimes permitting unbounded search, propagation, or lemma generation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nontermination Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nontermination caused by unrestricted restarts without persistent progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the satisfiable propositional instance \(F=p\), viewed as a degenerate DPLL(T) problem. Permit a scheduler to restart from the empty trail before making any decision or propagation, without learning a persistent clause. The infinite run \(\epsilon,\epsilon,\epsilon,\ldots\) is legal under that regime but never returns \(\mathsf{sat}\). Thus a finite input and a decidable theory do not ensure termination when restarts may indefinitely prevent progress; a fairness or well-founded progress requirement is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even the satisfiable instance p can loop forever if unrestricted restarts repeatedly erase the trail before any persistent progress occurs.
assumptions_latex: Restarts may occur before any decision or propagation.
No persistent progress measure must decrease across restarts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an infinite DPLL(T) run on the finite satisfiable input \(F=p\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and the example is valid under the stated permissive restart regime. A source is needed to establish that this run is legal for the intended DPLL(T) transition system.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Lemma Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic validity criterion for clauses learned from a theory solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a background theory \(T\), a theory lemma is a clause \(L=\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor\ell_k\) over theory literals. It is valid exactly when \(T\models L\), equivalently when \(T\land
eg L\) is unsatisfiable. Since \(
eg L\) equals \(
eg\ell_1\land\cdots\land
eg\ell_k\), a checkable unsatisfiability certificate for this conjunction modulo \(T\) certifies that adding \(L\) preserves the set of \(T\)-models of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learned theory clause is valid precisely when its negation is unsatisfiable modulo T; a checkable refutation certifies validity.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a clause over literals interpreted in the signature of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\models L\iff T\land\neg L\) is unsatisfiable.

notation.meaning: Theory literal occurring in the clause.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate-oriented validity criterion is mathematically standard and fits the node, but no authoritative source supports the theory-lemma definition or certification interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Conflict Explanation Soundness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity criterion for a theory solver's conflict explanation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be the current trail of asserted theory literals and let \(C\subseteq M\) be a reported conflict explanation. The explanation is sound when \(T\land\bigwedge_{\ell\in C}\ell\) is unsatisfiable. Equivalently, the conflict clause \(L_C=\bigvee_{\ell\in C}\neg\ell\) satisfies \(T\models L_C\). A verifiable theory-unsatisfiability certificate for the conjunction indexed by \(C\) therefore certifies both the conflict and the validity of the learned clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conflict explanation is sound when its literals are jointly T-inconsistent, making the disjunction of their negations a valid learned clause.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite subset of the current theory-literal trail \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\land\bigwedge_{\ell\in C}\ell\) is unsatisfiable if and only if \(T\models\bigvee_{\ell\in C}\neg\ell\).

notation.meaning: Clause learned from the conflict explanation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind and equivalence correctly express conflict-explanation soundness, but the record has no source for the DPLL(T) conflict interface or learned-clause criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Propagation Soundness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic condition for a theory-implied propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a consistent trail of theory literals and let \(\ell\) be an unassigned theory literal. Propagating \(\ell\) from an explanation \(C\subseteq M\) is sound exactly when \(T\land\bigwedge_{c\in C}c\models\ell\). Equivalently, \(T\land\bigwedge_{c\in C}c\land\neg\ell\) is unsatisfiable, and the explanation clause \(\bigvee_{c\in C}\neg c\lor\ell\) is \(T\)-valid. Hence adding the propagated literal cannot eliminate any model extending the explained trail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Theory propagation is sound when the explaining trail literals entail the propagated literal modulo T, equivalently when their conjunction with its negation is inconsistent.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq M\) is finite and \(T\land\bigwedge_{c\in C}c\) is satisfiable.
\(\ell\) is currently unassigned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\land\bigwedge_{c\in C}c\models\ell\), equivalently \(T\models\bigvee_{c\in C}\neg c\lor\ell\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property precisely states the semantic entailment required for sound theory propagation, but an authoritative source with a specific locator is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Theory Model Correctness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-validation criterion for a quantifier-free formula modulo one theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a quantifier-free formula in the signature of theory \(T\), and let \(\mathcal M\) be a returned total interpretation. The model is correct when \(\mathcal M\models T\) and evaluation of every atom of \(F\) in \(\mathcal M\) makes \(F\) true. A certificate may give interpretations of the symbols occurring in \(F\), together with checkable evidence that the relevant axioms of \(T\) and all asserted literals hold. Successful validation certifies \(\mathcal M\models T\land F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-theory model is correct when it satisfies the theory and its interpretation of the input atoms makes the entire formula true.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is quantifier-free in the signature of \(T\).
\(\mathcal M\) interprets every symbol occurring in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model validation succeeds only if \(\mathcal M\models T\land F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind is defensible for this model-validation leaf, and the semantic criterion is coherent. The proposed certificate and validation requirements nevertheless lack authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined-Model Correctness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nelson–Oppen-style model combination for disjoint stably infinite theories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) be stably infinite theories with disjoint nonlogical signatures and shared equality. Let \(\Gamma_i\) be finite sets of ground \(T_i\)-literals obtained after purification, and let \(V\) be their shared variables. If \(E\) is a complete, consistent arrangement of equalities and disequalities over \(V\), and each \(T_i\land\Gamma_i\land E\) has a model, then component models can be chosen with matching equality classes on \(V\) and combined into an interpretation \(\mathcal M\) satisfying \((T_1\cup T_2)\land\Gamma_1\land\Gamma_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For disjoint stably infinite theories, satisfiable purified components sharing a consistent complete equality arrangement combine into a model of their union.
assumptions_latex: \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are stably infinite and have disjoint nonlogical signatures.
\(E\) is a complete consistent equality arrangement over the shared variables.
Each \(T_i\land\Gamma_i\land E\) is satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\mathcal M\models(T_1\cup T_2)\land\Gamma_1\land\Gamma_2\).

notation.meaning: Purified ground literals belonging to component theory i.
Variables shared by the purified components.
Complete arrangement of equalities and disequalities over shared variables.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits combined-model correctness and states the standard disjoint, stably infinite setting, but the model-combination conclusion is nontrivial and requires an authoritative Nelson–Oppen source with a theorem or section locator.

children.title: Partial-Model Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on interpretation coverage in solver-produced partial models.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Model Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a displayed partial assignment and a semantic SMT model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a closed SMT formula over signature \(\Sigma\), and let \(p\) assign values to only a subset \(D\) of the relevant constants or ground terms. The partial assignment \(p\) is not by itself a satisfiability certificate unless either \(p\) is accompanied by a total \(\Sigma\)-structure \(M\) with \(M\models F\), or every theory-consistent total extension \(M\supseteq p\) satisfies \(F\). If some consistent extensions satisfy \(F\) and others falsify it, the displayed information lies beyond the certification boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial assignment certifies satisfiability only through a satisfying completion or when every theory-consistent completion satisfies the formula; otherwise it is inconclusive.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a closed formula with standard theory semantics.
\(p\) is type-correct and theory-consistent on its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) certifies \(F\) only if \((\exists M\supseteq p)(M\models F)\) is witnessed or \((\forall M\supseteq p)(M\models F)\).

notation.meaning: total theory structure extending the assignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematical distinction between a partial display and a satisfying total completion are appropriate, but no cited source supports the chosen completion and certification semantics.

children.title: Unknown-Result Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which the solver returns neither satisfiable nor unsatisfiable.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Result Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical guarantees attached to an SMT solver's unknown response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an SMT instance \(F\), a sound three-valued solver response has the contracts \(\operatorname{res}(F)=\mathsf{sat}\Rightarrow F\) is satisfiable and \(\operatorname{res}(F)=\mathsf{unsat}\Rightarrow F\) is unsatisfiable. The response \(\operatorname{res}(F)=\mathsf{unknown}\) entails neither conclusion: absent an independently checkable certificate, it is compatible with both \(F\) being satisfiable and \(F\) being unsatisfiable. Any candidate assignment returned with \(\mathsf{unknown}\) remains noncertifying until independently completed and checked against \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown means that neither satisfiability nor unsatisfiability has been established. Any accompanying assignment requires independent validation before it becomes a certificate.
assumptions_latex: The solver uses the result values \(\mathsf{sat}\), \(\mathsf{unsat}\), and \(\mathsf{unknown}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{res}(F)=\mathsf{unknown}\not\Rightarrow F\in\mathsf{SAT}\) and \(\operatorname{res}(F)=\mathsf{unknown}\not\Rightarrow F\in\mathsf{UNSAT}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits and the logical treatment of unknown is sound, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the solver-result contract or treatment of accompanying assignments.

children.title: Partial-Model Interpretability
children.top_down_role: Permitted uses and trust limits for incomplete model information.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Model Interpretability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition under which values displayed or omitted by a partial SMT model have stable semantic meaning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a closed SMT formula and let \(p:D\to V\) be a type-correct partial assignment having at least one theory-consistent total extension satisfying \(F\). A displayed entry \(p(t)\), for \(t\in D\), is semantically faithful when every satisfying total extension \(M\supseteq p\) has \(\llbracket t\rrbracket_M=p(t)\). More generally, a term \(u\), whether or not \(u\in D\), has a completion-independent value relative to \(F\) and \(p\) exactly when all satisfying total extensions of \(p\) assign the same value to \(u\). If two such extensions assign different values to \(u\), its value is not determined by the partial model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A displayed value is faithful when every satisfying total extension agrees with it. Any displayed or omitted term has a stable value exactly when all satisfying extensions agree on that value; disagreement makes the term undetermined by the partial model.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a closed SMT formula with fixed theory semantics.
\(p:D\to V\) is type-correct and has at least one theory-consistent total extension satisfying \(F\).
