knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For any term \(u\), completion-independent interpretability is equivalent to \((\forall M_1,M_2\supseteq p)\bigl((M_1\models F\land M_2\models F)\Rightarrow \llbracket u\rrbracket_{M_1}=\llbracket u\rrbracket_{M_2}\bigr)\); for \(u\in D\), faithfulness additionally requires this common value to equal \(p(u)\).

notation.meaning: domain of the displayed partial assignment
value of term u in total structure M

children.title: Unknown-Cause Classification
children.top_down_role: Sources of unknown outcomes across unsupported, incomplete, or resource-limited reasoning.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Cause Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational classification of unknown outcomes without changing their logical status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an SMT run on \(F\) returning \(\mathsf{unknown}\), record a diagnostic label \(c\) from \(\{\mathsf{incomplete},\mathsf{resource},\mathsf{interrupted},\mathsf{unsupported},\mathsf{numerical},\mathsf{other}\}\). These labels respectively denote an incomplete decision procedure, exhausted time or memory, external interruption, unsupported input features, unreliable numerical reasoning, or an unclassified cause. The label is operational metadata: for every \(c\), the pair \((\mathsf{unknown},c)\) entails neither \(F\)'s satisfiability nor its unsatisfiability without a separately checked certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown causes may be classified operationally, but no cause label changes unknown into a logical satisfiability or unsatisfiability result.
assumptions_latex: The run terminates with \(\operatorname{res}(F)=\mathsf{unknown}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{res}(F),c)=(\mathsf{unknown},c)\) carries diagnostic information only and decides neither \(F\in\mathsf{SAT}\) nor \(F\in\mathsf{UNSAT}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate kind for an operational classification, and the logical-status caveat is correct. The particular label set is a proposed normalization, however, and has no standard or solver-specific citation.

children.title: Model Certificates
children.top_down_role: Interpretations supplied as evidence for satisfiable SMT results.

knowledge_statements.title: Model Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic certificate for an SMT satisfiable result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a closed formula over a many-sorted signature \(\Sigma\) and background theory \(T\). A model certificate is a finite representation \(C\) from which a checker reconstructs a total \(\Sigma\)-structure \(M_C\) such that \(M_C\models T\) and \(M_C\models F\). Verification consists of checking sort correctness, interpretations of symbols needed by \(F\), satisfaction of the relevant theory constraints, and evaluation \(\llbracket F\rrbracket_{M_C}=\mathsf{true}\). Acceptance certifies that \(F\) is \(T\)-satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model certificate reconstructs a total theory model in which the input formula evaluates to true; successful independent checking certifies satisfiability.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is closed and all its symbols have declared sorts.
The checker implements the semantics of the background theory \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CheckModel}(F,C)=\mathsf{accept}\Rightarrow (\exists M_C)(M_C\models T\land M_C\models F)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct role, and the statement gives a coherent semantic acceptance condition. An authoritative source is required for the finite representation, reconstruction, and checking requirements.

children.title: Value Assignments
children.top_down_role: Reported values for constants, terms, functions, or other model-visible entities.

knowledge_statements.title: Value Assignments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed value assignments used in SMT model certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a many-sorted signature \(\Sigma\) with carrier \(D_s\) for each sort \(s\), a value assignment on a set \(X\) of sorted constants is a function \(\alpha:X\to\bigcup_s D_s\) satisfying \(\alpha(x)\in D_s\) whenever \(x\) has sort \(s\). Relative to a structure \(M\), the assignment extends to terms recursively: constants use \(\alpha\) or their interpretation in \(M\), and \(\llbracket f(t_1,\ldots,t_k)\rrbracket_{M,\alpha}=f^M(\llbracket t_1\rrbracket_{M,\alpha},\ldots,\llbracket t_k\rrbracket_{M,\alpha})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value assignment maps each assigned constant to a value of its declared sort and extends compositionally to compound terms within a structure.
assumptions_latex: Every symbol in \(X\) has a declared sort.
\(M\) interprets the function symbols occurring in evaluated terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(x)\in D_{\operatorname{sort}(x)}\) for every \(x\in X\), with term values defined compositionally.

notation.meaning: interpretation of function symbol f in M

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent as certificate-oriented terminology, but assigning constants through an auxiliary assignment rather than solely through their structure interpretation is format-specific and needs a cited many-sorted semantics or certificate specification.

children.title: Assignment-Coverage Regimes
children.top_down_role: Partial versus total coverage of requested model values.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-Coverage Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage classes for assignment certificates used to evaluate closed quantifier-free SMT formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a closed quantifier-free SMT formula, let \(R(F)\) be the finite set of ground subterms whose values are encountered during compositional evaluation of \(F\), and let \(C\) be a certificate that explicitly assigns values to a set \(D\subseteq R(F)\) and may also provide interpretations from which further required values can be computed. Coverage is explicit-total when \(D=R(F)\). It is evaluation-complete when a deterministic certificate evaluator can compute \(\llbracket t\rrbracket\) for every \(t\in R(F)\) from the explicit assignments and represented symbol interpretations. It is partial when the evaluator cannot determine at least one required term value. Direct checking of \(F\) is possible in the first two regimes; partial coverage requires additional model information or a separately checked satisfying completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed quantifier-free formula, coverage is explicit-total when every required ground subterm is assigned, evaluation-complete when all required values can be computed from the certificate, and partial otherwise. Direct evaluation is available only in the first two regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is closed and quantifier-free.
\(R(F)\) is the finite set of ground subterms visited by the specified compositional evaluator.
The certificate format defines how explicit values and represented symbol interpretations are decoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Direct evaluation of \(F\) from \(C\) is available when \(D=R(F)\) or when the certificate evaluator computes \(\llbracket t\rrbracket\) for every \(t\in R(F)\); otherwise the coverage is partial.

notation.meaning: required ground subterms encountered during evaluation of F
assignment certificate and any represented symbol interpretations
subset of required terms with explicitly represented values

children.title: Model–Assignment Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency between reported term values and the encompassing model interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Model–Assignment Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agreement condition between a model structure and its displayed assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a many-sorted structure and \(\alpha:D\to\bigcup_s D_s^M\) a displayed assignment for constants or ground terms. The pair \((M,\alpha)\) is model–assignment consistent exactly when every assigned value is sort-correct and \(\alpha(t)=\llbracket t\rrbracket_M\) for all \(t\in D\). If \(M\models F\), consistency makes \(\alpha\) a faithful projection of the satisfying model; disagreement for even one covered term invalidates the combined certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model and displayed assignment are consistent exactly when every assigned term has the same, correctly sorted value under the model.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) interprets every symbol occurring in each \(t\in D\).
\(\alpha\) assigns a value to every term in \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Consistent}(M,\alpha)\iff (\forall t\in D)\,\alpha(t)=\llbracket t\rrbracket_M\) with matching sorts.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct role, and equality between displayed values and term evaluations states the intended consistency requirement. The certificate convention and model-evaluation semantics remain uncited.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsatisfiable Cores
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset certificate localizing inconsistency in a finite SMT assertion set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n\}\) be a finite set of asserted formulas interpreted in background theory \(T\). An unsatisfiable core is a subset \(C\subseteq A\) such that no \(T\)-model satisfies every formula in \(C\), equivalently \(T\models\neg\bigwedge_{\varphi\in C}\varphi\). It is minimal when every proper subset of \(C\) is \(T\)-satisfiable. A core identifies sufficient inconsistent input but is not independently checkable unless accompanied by a refutation or checked by a trusted decision procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsatisfiable core is an inconsistent subset of asserted formulas. Minimality additionally requires every proper subset to be satisfiable.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is finite.
All formulas are interpreted in the same background theory \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\subseteq A\) and \(T\models\neg\bigwedge_{\varphi\in C}\varphi\); minimality requires \((\forall C'\subsetneq C)\,C'\) to be \(T\)-satisfiable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Within the SMT certificate-family container, certificate is an acceptable role. The core and subset-minimal-core definitions are standard and precise, but no authoritative source supports them or the independent-checkability qualification.

children.title: SMT Proof Traces
children.top_down_role: Recorded inference artifacts emitted during SMT solving.

knowledge_statements.title: SMT Proof Traces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logged derivations intended to justify an SMT unsatisfiable result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For assertions \(A\) in theory \(T\), an SMT proof trace is a finite sequence \(\pi=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)\) of records containing derived clauses or formulas, references to premises, and inference-rule identifiers. Each initial record must be justified by \(A\) or valid theory axioms, and each subsequent record must follow from earlier records under its named rule. A trace is refutational when its final record is \(\bot\). The trace certifies unsatisfiability only relative to a checker that validates every represented rule and theory lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SMT proof trace records premises and inference steps ending in contradiction. It certifies unsatisfiability only when every step and theory lemma is checkable.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite assertion set in theory \(T\).
All premise references in \(\pi\) are acyclic and precede their uses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every step of \(\pi\) is valid and \(r_m=\bot\), then \(A\) is \(T\)-unsatisfiable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate fits the trace container, and the conditional refutational claim is coherent. Proof-trace record structure and theory-lemma checking vary by format and require a specific authoritative citation.

children.title: Checkable Refutations
children.top_down_role: Unsatisfiability artifacts structured for independent verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Checkable Refutations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel-checkable derivations of contradiction from SMT assertions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be assertions in theory \(T\), and let \(R\) be a finite derivation whose leaves are members of \(A\) or checker-recognized \(T\)-valid lemmas. The refutation is checkable when every internal node is obtained from its cited predecessors by a decidable, sound inference predicate \(\operatorname{ValidStep}\), and the root is \(\bot\). A checker accepting all leaves, steps, and the contradictory root certifies \(A\models_T\bot\), hence that \(A\) is \(T\)-unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A checkable refutation is a finite derivation whose leaves and inference steps are decidably validated and whose root is contradiction.
assumptions_latex: The step predicate \(\operatorname{ValidStep}\) is sound for theory \(T\).
All referenced premises occur in the finite derivation \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CheckRefutation}(A,R)=\mathsf{accept}\Rightarrow A\models_T\bot\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct role and the sound-checker implication is mathematically appropriate. The leaf-validation and inference-checking framework lacks an authoritative proof-certificate source.

children.title: Trace-to-Refutation Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Conversion of solver traces into complete checkable refutation artifacts.

knowledge_statements.title: Trace-to-Refutation Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstructing an explicit refutation DAG from an SMT proof trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input assertions \(A\), theory \(T\), and trace \(\pi=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)\). Initialize a map \(N\) with nodes for asserted premises. Process records in order: decode the conclusion \(C_i\), resolve every premise reference through \(N\), instantiate the named inference rule, validate its side conditions, and store the resulting derivation node as \(N[i]\). Reject on an unresolved reference, invalid theory lemma, failed side condition, or mismatched conclusion. If the final reconstructed node has conclusion \(\bot\), output its reachable derivation DAG \(R\); otherwise report that no refutation was reconstructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decode each trace step, resolve premises, validate its rule, and build a derivation DAG. Output a refutation only when the final validated conclusion is contradiction.
assumptions_latex: Trace records are processed in dependency order.
The reconstructor implements every rule identifier occurring in \(\pi\).
Theory-lemma side conditions are decidable by the checker.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(R\) only if every reconstructed step is valid and \(\operatorname{root}(R)=\bot\).

notation.meaning: map from trace identifiers to derivation nodes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind, but the procedure is only a format-parametric reconstruction schema. Its decoding, rule instantiation, side conditions, and correctness cannot be evaluated without a specific trace format and reconstruction source.

children.title: Refutation-Checkability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Format, theory-support, plus reconstruction limits affecting independent checking.

knowledge_statements.title: Refutation-Checkability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of independently checking SMT refutations containing theory-specific inference steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be an SMT formula, \(\pi\) a finite claimed refutation, and \(K\) a total checker. The implication \(K(F,\pi)=\mathsf{accept}\Rightarrow F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\) holds only relative to the soundness of every primitive rule and side-condition procedure used by \(K\). If a theory lemma \(L\) is accepted without a checkable derivation or a verified decision procedure establishing \(T\models L\), then acceptance certifies unsatisfiability only relative to that trusted lemma oracle. Consequently, proof logging alone does not yield an independently checkable refutation when opaque theory lemmas cross the checker boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A refutation is independently checkable only when every inference, including each theory lemma, has a sound effective check; opaque lemmas enlarge the trusted base.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) is finite and every recorded inference has a specified conclusion and premises.
\(K\) terminates on every pair \((F,\pi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(F,\pi)=\mathsf{accept}\Rightarrow \operatorname{Unsat}_T(F)\) only relative to all unchecked theory oracles invoked by \(K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but no cited proof-format or checker-soundness source supports the precise trusted-oracle boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Craig Interpolants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic Craig interpolation for an inconsistent pair of first-order formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be first-order formulas such that \(A\land B\) is unsatisfiable. A Craig interpolant for the ordered pair \((A,B)\) is a formula \(I\) satisfying \(A\models I\), \(I\land B\models\bot\), and \(\operatorname{sig}(I)\subseteq \operatorname{sig}(A)\cap\operatorname{sig}(B)\), where \(\operatorname{sig}\) contains the nonlogical symbols of a formula. In an SMT theory \(T\), the corresponding conditions are \(T\models A\rightarrow I\) and \(T\models \neg(I\land B)\), with the permitted shared theory symbols fixed by the interpolation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interpolant follows from one part of an inconsistent pair, contradicts the other part, and uses only their shared nonlogical vocabulary.
assumptions_latex: \(A\land B\models\bot\), or \(T\models\neg(A\land B)\) in the theory-relative form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\models I\), \(I\land B\models\bot\), and \(\operatorname{sig}(I)\subseteq\operatorname{sig}(A)\cap\operatorname{sig}(B)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit Craig interpolants, but no source with a specific definition, theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: SAT-Layer Proof Logging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clause-level logging of the Boolean abstraction used by an SMT solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Boolean abstraction with initial clause set \(C_0\), a SAT-layer proof log is a finite sequence \((s_1,\ldots,s_m)\). Each step either adds a clause \(C_i\) justified from currently active clauses by the declared propositional rule, or deletes a clause without changing the represented derivability claim. Typical admissible additions satisfy resolution, reverse unit propagation, or the resolution asymmetric tautology condition. The log represents a refutation when its final active derivation contains the empty clause \(\bot\). In SMT, clauses encoding theory lemmas must additionally identify the theory justification required outside the SAT layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A SAT proof log records checkable clause additions and optional deletions until the empty clause is derived; theory-lemma clauses require separate justification.
assumptions_latex: \(C_0\) is the clausified Boolean abstraction of the input.
Every clause-addition rule has a deterministic checking predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bot\in\operatorname{closure}(C_0;s_1,\ldots,s_m)\) certifies propositional unsatisfiability when every addition check succeeds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits, but resolution, RUP, and RAT belong to distinct proof-system specifications; an authoritative locator is needed to delimit the intended logging format and deletion semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Proof Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstructing explicit theory derivations from an SMT solver’s coarse proof trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an SMT formula \(F\), a coarse refutation trace \(\tau\), and a checker for the background theory \(T\). Traverse \(\tau\) in dependency order. Retain each valid propositional inference. For every asserted theory lemma \(L\), construct a derivation \(d_L\) from its recorded theory premises and accept it only if the theory checker establishes \(T\models L\). Replace the coarse lemma step by \(d_L\), then recheck all dependent inferences. Output the resulting derivation \(\pi\) if its final conclusion is \(\bot\); otherwise return reconstruction failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reconstruction expands each coarse theory lemma into a checker-approved derivation, preserves valid propositional steps, and succeeds only when the resulting proof ends in contradiction.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau\) has an acyclic dependency order and ends with a claimed contradiction.
The theory checker is sound for every reconstructed theory rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reconstruct}(F,\tau,T)=\pi\Rightarrow \operatorname{concl}(\pi)=\bot\) and every step of \(\pi\) passes its designated checker.

notation.meaning: Reconstructed derivation of theory lemma L

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but the method for constructing each derivation and the theory calculus checked are unspecified, so the claimed reconstruction procedure requires a format-specific source.

children.title: Integrated Proof Formats
children.top_down_role: Monolithic formats combining SAT-level and theory-level proof evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrated Proof Formats
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-calculus proof objects combining Boolean and theory reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integrated SMT proof format represents a proof as one directed acyclic graph \(P=(V,E)\) governed by a common inference calculus \(\mathcal R\). Each node records a formula or clause, its predecessor nodes, and a rule in \(\mathcal R\); the rule set includes both propositional and theory-specific inferences. A checker accepts a claimed refutation exactly when every node is well formed, every local rule instance is valid, all references are acyclic and available, and the designated root is \(\bot\). No separate semantic boundary between SAT and theory proof objects is exposed by the format.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrated format places propositional and theory inferences in one proof graph and one rule language, with local checks leading to an empty-clause root.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is finite and its dependency relation \(E\) is acyclic.
Every rule in \(\mathcal R\) has a specified local checking predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}_{\mathcal R}(P)=\mathsf{accept}\) exactly when all local checks succeed and \(\operatorname{root}(P)=\bot\).

notation.meaning: Combined propositional and theory rule set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits, but the asserted common-calculus characterization and absence of a separate SAT–theory boundary require an authoritative proof-format taxonomy source.

children.title: Modular Proof Formats
children.top_down_role: Formats partitioning proof evidence across cooperating modules.

knowledge_statements.title: Modular Proof Formats
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composed proof objects with separately checked SAT and theory modules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A modular SMT proof format represents a refutation as \(P=(P_B,(P_j)_{j\in J},I)\), where \(P_B\) is a Boolean proof, each \(P_j\) is a proof in a theory-specific calculus, and \(I\) maps imported or exported conclusions to their occurrences across modules. The composite checker accepts only if every module checker accepts, every interface reference preserves the identical formula under an agreed serialization and symbol context, dependencies between modules are acyclic, and the Boolean top-level proof concludes \(\bot\). Sound composition additionally requires each accepted exported conclusion to follow from its declared imported premises.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A modular format combines separately checked Boolean and theory proofs through explicit formula-preserving interfaces and accepts only when their composition derives contradiction.
assumptions_latex: Each module checker is sound for its declared calculus.
The interface map \(I\) preserves formulas, symbol contexts, and dependency order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}(P)=\mathsf{accept}\Rightarrow \operatorname{concl}(P_B)=\bot\), relative to the soundness of all module checkers and interface checks.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits, but this particular Boolean-module, theory-module, and interface-map model is not supported by a cited modular proof-format specification.

children.title: Proof-Module Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Exchange boundaries linking independently produced proof components.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Module Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness conditions for exchanging formulas and derivations between proof modules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let modules \(M_i\) exchange obligations through interface records \((\Gamma,\varphi,\sigma)\), where \(\Gamma\) lists imported premises, \(\varphi\) is the exported conclusion, and \(\sigma\) fixes the symbol, sort, and term encoding. A proof-module interface is sound when every accepted export satisfies \(\Gamma\models_{T_i}\varphi\); sender and receiver interpret \(\sigma\) identically; every imported premise is linked to an accepted export or an original assumption; and the resulting intermodule dependency graph is acyclic. Under these conditions, composing sound module derivations preserves semantic consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound module interface preserves formulas and typing, links every premise to an approved source, prevents cyclic justification, and exports only semantic consequences.
assumptions_latex: Every module \(M_i\) has a sound local proof checker.
All exchanged records use a shared or explicitly translated signature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\forall i,\ \Gamma_i\models_{T_i}\varphi_i\bigr)\land\operatorname{Acyclic}(I)\Rightarrow\operatorname{SoundComposition}(M_1,\ldots,M_k,I)\).

notation.meaning: Premises, exported conclusion, and encoding context

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but local consequences under possibly different theories do not alone establish global sound composition without explicit shared-semantics or translation conditions. A format-specific source is required.

children.title: Proof Checker Architectures
children.top_down_role: Architectural choices for consuming and validating SMT proof artifacts.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof Checker Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional decomposition of an SMT proof checker into parsing, reconstruction, and trusted validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proof checker architecture can be represented by functions \(D\), \(R\), and \(K\). The decoder \(D\) maps an external proof artifact \(b\) to a typed proof object or rejects it; the optional reconstructor \(R\) expands derived or implicit steps; and the kernel \(K\) validates primitive inferences. Overall acceptance is defined by \(\operatorname{Check}(F,b)=K(F,R(D(b)))\), with rejection propagated from any stage. In a monolithic architecture these functions share one trusted implementation; in a kernel architecture, only the decoder-to-kernel representation boundary and \(K\) need belong to the trusted computing base.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Checker architectures decode proof artifacts, optionally reconstruct omitted steps, and validate primitive inferences; their organization determines which components must be trusted.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted external artifact has a unique well-typed interpretation passed to \(K\).
Reconstruction preserves the conclusion and declared assumptions of the decoded proof.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Check}(F,b)=\mathsf{accept}\Rightarrow K(F,R(D(b)))=\mathsf{accept}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits, but the claim that only the representation boundary and kernel are trusted is valid only if reconstructed output is independently validated by the kernel. The stated assumptions do not establish this, and no architecture source is cited.

children.title: Trusted-Kernel Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Placement and extent of components included in the trusted computing base.

knowledge_statements.title: Trusted-Kernel Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trusted computing base induced by the acceptance path of a proof checker.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a checker whose acceptance computation has components \(C_1,\ldots,C_n\), the trusted-kernel boundary is the partition \((\mathcal T,\mathcal U)\) such that the soundness claim \(\operatorname{Check}(F,p)=\mathsf{accept}\Rightarrow\operatorname{Unsat}(F)\) depends on the correct implementation or verified specification of every component in \(\mathcal T\), while outputs from components in \(\mathcal U\) are validated before affecting acceptance. Parsers, arithmetic routines, theory decision procedures, axiom tables, and proof reconstruction belong to \(\mathcal T\) whenever malformed or unsound outputs from them can cause acceptance without subsequent validation by the trusted kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trusted-kernel boundary separates components whose correctness soundness depends on from untrusted components whose outputs are fully validated before acceptance.
assumptions_latex: The checker’s acceptance dataflow and all validation dependencies are specified.
Soundness means that acceptance implies unsatisfiability of the checked formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_i\in\mathcal U\) only if every acceptance-relevant output of \(C_i\) is validated by components in \(\mathcal T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but the proposed partition and component-membership criterion require a trusted-computing-base or proof-checker architecture source with a specific locator.

children.title: Checker–Kernel Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Evidence-transfer boundaries between proof checkers and trusted kernels.

knowledge_statements.title: Checker–Kernel Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity conditions at the boundary between an untrusted checker front end and a trusted kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an untrusted front end emit a kernel request \(q=(\Gamma,r,\varphi,\sigma)\), containing premise identifiers, a primitive rule, a conclusion, and a typing context. A checker–kernel interface is sound when the kernel independently parses or safely decodes \(q\), resolves every premise to a previously accepted theorem, verifies all sorts and symbols under \(\sigma\), and accepts only if its implementation of \(r\) derives \(\varphi\) from \(\Gamma\). Requests may reference no mutable or unchecked semantic state. Thus arbitrary front-end behavior cannot create a kernel theorem except through an accepted primitive inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound checker–kernel interface uses typed requests, accepted premises, immutable semantics, and independent kernel validation of every primitive inference.
assumptions_latex: The kernel’s primitive rules are sound.
Previously accepted theorem identifiers are immutable and unambiguous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(q)=\mathsf{accept}\Rightarrow \Gamma\models\varphi\), independently of the behavior of the untrusted front end.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but the immutable-state, decoding, typing, and primitive-rule requirements describe a particular kernel model for which no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Tractable Specialized Fragments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time propositional fragments viewed as specialized empty-theory SMT instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a propositional CNF formula with \(n\) variables and \(m\) literal occurrences. If every clause of \(F\) contains at most one positive literal, Horn satisfiability is decidable by forward chaining in time \(O(n+m)\). If every clause contains at most two literals, 2-SAT is decidable by constructing the implication graph and testing its strongly connected components in time \(O(n+m)\). These are tractable specialized SMT fragments over the empty theory, although unrestricted Boolean combinations recover NP-complete SAT.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horn-SAT and 2-SAT are linear-time specialized fragments, solved respectively by forward chaining and implication-graph strongly connected components.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is represented explicitly as a CNF formula.
The unit-cost RAM model charges constant time per literal or graph edge operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{time}_{\mathrm{Horn}}(F)=O(n+m)\) and \(\operatorname{time}_{\mathrm{2SAT}}(F)=O(n+m)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, and the Horn-SAT and 2-SAT bounds are standard, but neither bound has the required textbook section, theorem, or page citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard Quantifier-Free Fragments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness of quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider satisfiability of quantifier-free formulas formed by Boolean combinations of linear inequalities \(a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n\le b\), where \(x_i\in\mathbb Z\) and all integer coefficients are encoded in binary. This problem, commonly denoted \(\mathrm{QF\_LIA}\)-SAT, is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. NP-hardness already holds through the encoding of Boolean choices by bounded integer variables, while membership in NP uses the polynomial-size solution property for feasible integer linear systems selected by a satisfying Boolean structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Satisfiability for quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic with binary-encoded coefficients is NP-complete, despite containing no quantifiers.
assumptions_latex: Variables range over \(\mathbb Z\), and coefficients and bounds are binary encoded.
Formula size includes the Boolean syntax and coefficient bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{QF\_LIA}\text{-SAT}\) is \(\mathsf{NP}\)-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, but the exact NP-completeness classification for binary-encoded QF_LIA, including its NP-membership assumptions, needs an authoritative theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Decidable Quantified Fragments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-theoretic definition for satisfiability of closed quantified formulas in a fixed theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a theory and \(\mathcal F\) a recursively recognizable class of closed, possibly quantified, formulas over the signature of \(T\). The fragment \(\mathcal F\) is decidable modulo \(T\) if there exists an algorithm \(D\) that halts on every \(\varphi\in\mathcal F\) and returns \(\mathsf{sat}\) exactly when \(T\cup\{\varphi\}\) has a model, and otherwise returns \(\mathsf{unsat}\). Thus both satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances receive terminating, correct answers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantified fragment is decidable when one terminating algorithm correctly classifies every formula in it as satisfiable or unsatisfiable modulo the fixed theory.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) has an effective signature and \(\mathcal F\) is recursively recognizable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\varphi\in\mathcal F,\ D(\varphi)\downarrow\in\{\mathsf{sat},\mathsf{unsat}\}\) with the stated model-theoretic correctness.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, precise, and appropriate for the Decidable Quantified Fragments container, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Semidecidable Fragments
children.top_down_role: Fragments supporting one-sided termination guarantees.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) and its formula encoding are effective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(\varphi)\downarrow=\mathsf{accept}\) if and only if \(T\cup\{\varphi\}\) is satisfiable; on an unsatisfiable input, \(A\) may reject or diverge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive semidecidability of satisfiability modulo a fixed theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a theory and \(\mathcal F\) an effective class of closed formulas. Satisfiability for \(\mathcal F\) modulo \(T\) is semidecidable if there exists an algorithm \(A\) such that, for every \(\varphi\in\mathcal F\), \(A(\varphi)\) halts and accepts if and only if \(T\cup\{\varphi\}\) is satisfiable; when that set is unsatisfiable, \(A(\varphi)\) may reject or run forever. Equivalently, under an effective encoding, the satisfiable members of \(\mathcal F\) form a recursively enumerable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fragment is satisfiability-semidecidable when a sound procedure eventually accepts every satisfiable input, while it may reject or run forever on an unsatisfiable input.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidecidable Fragments

children.title: Undecidable Fragments
children.top_down_role: Fragments lying beyond complete decision procedures.

knowledge_statements.title: Undecidable Fragments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undecidability of satisfiability for an effective SMT fragment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a theory and \(\mathcal F\) an effective class of closed formulas. Satisfiability for \(\mathcal F\) modulo \(T\) is undecidable if no algorithm halts on every \(\varphi\in\mathcal F\) and correctly determines whether \(T\cup\{\varphi\}\) has a model. Undecidability does not by itself exclude a one-sided semidecision procedure; it excludes only a total correct classifier for both satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fragment is undecidable when no terminating algorithm can correctly classify every instance, even though one outcome may still be semidecidable.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) has an effective finite encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists D\ \forall\varphi\in\mathcal F:\ D(\varphi)\downarrow\) and \(D\) decides satisfiability modulo \(T\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes undecidability from failure of one-sided semidecidability and fits the terminal container, but it has no inspectable source.

children.title: Decidability Boundary Transitions
children.top_down_role: Language extensions or theory features that cross computability boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Decidability Boundary Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary witnessed by a decidable fragment whose effective extension is undecidable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\subsetneq\mathcal G\) be effective formula fragments over the same theory \(T\). A decidability boundary transition occurs when satisfiability modulo \(T\) is decidable on \(\mathcal F\) but undecidable on \(\mathcal G\). If \(\mathcal G\) is obtained by admitting a feature \(q\), then \(q\) is boundary-crossing relative to \(\mathcal F\): every instance in \(\mathcal F\) remains decidable, whereas no total correct decision procedure covers all formulas generated after admitting \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a syntactic or semantic feature crosses a decidability boundary when the smaller fragment is decidable but the resulting larger fragment is not.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\subsetneq\mathcal G\) are effective fragments over one fixed theory \(T\).
Satisfiability on \(\mathcal F\) is decidable and satisfiability on \(\mathcal G\) is undecidable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\subsetneq\mathcal G\) witnesses a decidability boundary, and the extension feature has no total decision procedure on \(\mathcal G\).

notation.meaning: Feature admitted by the larger fragment.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract boundary-transition formulation is coherent and the failure_boundary kind fits, but no source supports this terminology or a concrete decidable-to-undecidable extension exhibiting it.

children.title: Encoding Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity attributable to translating SMT problems into solver-facing representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size and computation overhead of reducing source instances to SMT formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an encoding \(E\) mapping an instance \(I\) to an equisatisfiable SMT formula \(E(I)\), define its size overhead by \(s_E(n)=\max_{|I|\le n}|E(I)|\) and its construction time by \(t_E(n)=\max_{|I|\le n}\operatorname{time}(E,I)\). The encoding is polynomial if polynomials \(p\) and \(q\) satisfy \(s_E(n)\le p(n)\) and \(t_E(n)\le q(n)\) for every \(n\). A superpolynomial \(s_E\) can dominate downstream solver complexity even when the encoded fragment is tractable in formula length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding complexity measures both construction time and output size; a large representation blow-up can dominate the cost of solving the encoded formula.
assumptions_latex: \(|I|\) and \(|E(I)|\) denote bit lengths under fixed effective encodings.
\(E(I)\) preserves the intended satisfiability answer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\) is polynomial exactly when \(s_E\) and \(t_E\) admit polynomial upper bounds.

children.title: Theory-Combination Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity introduced by coordinating multiple background theories.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-Combination Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arrangement-enumeration bound for combining two disjoint stably infinite theories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let quantifier-free \(\varphi_1\land\varphi_2\) use disjoint theory signatures except for \(m\) shared variables, and let both component theories be decidable and stably infinite. An arrangement-based combination procedure may enumerate equivalence relations on those variables. Since their number is the Bell number \(B_m\), a direct deterministic implementation has the upper bound \(O(B_m(C_1(n)+C_2(n)+\operatorname{poly}(n)))\), where \(C_i(n)\) bounds one consistency check in theory \(i\). This is an algorithmic upper bound, not a matching lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct theory combination may test every equality arrangement of shared variables, multiplying component decision costs by a Bell-number factor.
assumptions_latex: The component signatures are disjoint apart from equality and shared variables.
Both component theories are decidable and stably infinite.
The input is purified into component constraints of total length \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{comb}}(n,m)=O(B_m(C_1(n)+C_2(n)+\operatorname{poly}(n)))\) for exhaustive arrangement enumeration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The arrangement intuition is standard, but the exact Bell-number runtime bound depends on the purification size, arrangement representation, per-arrangement constraint growth, and component-oracle cost model. No Nelson-Oppen or complexity source is supplied to justify the displayed bound.

children.title: Encoding–Combination Interaction Costs
children.top_down_role: Cost regimes arising from the interaction between encodings and theory combination.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding–Combination Interaction Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional upper bound exposing shared-variable growth caused by encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an encoder \(E\) produce a purified combined-theory formula of length \(N=s_E(n)\) with \(m_E(n)\) variables shared between theory components. If arrangement enumeration is used and component checks cost \(C_1(N)\) and \(C_2(N)\), then the end-to-end time is bounded by \(t_E(n)+O(B_{m_E(n)}(C_1(N)+C_2(N)+\operatorname{poly}(N)))\). Thus a polynomial-size encoding can still induce superpolynomial combination overhead when it creates an unbounded number of shared variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding and combination costs interact through encoded size and the number of shared variables, which may cause Bell-number growth despite polynomial encoding size.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) preserves satisfiability and produces a purified two-theory formula.
The arrangement-based combination assumptions hold for the component theories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{total}}(n)\le t_E(n)+O(B_{m_E(n)}(C_1(s_E(n))+C_2(s_E(n))+\operatorname{poly}(s_E(n))))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compositional expression fits the interaction-cost container, but it inherits the unsupported arrangement bound and additionally requires evidence that the encoder-induced shared-variable count enters the combination cost exactly as stated.

children.title: Worst-Case Complexity
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic hardness across SMT fragments and solver families.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic worst-case running time as a function of encoded input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a terminating deterministic solver \(A\), its worst-case running time at length \(n\) is \(W_A(n)=\max\{\operatorname{time}_A(x):|x|=n\}\), with the maximum replaced by a supremum if necessary. The solver has worst-case upper bound \(O(f(n))\) when constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\) exist such that \(W_A(n)\le c f(n)\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). This measure ranges over all encoded instances and does not predict a particular workload distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case complexity is the maximum runtime over all inputs of a given encoded length and need not describe typical solver behavior.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) terminates on every input in the considered fragment.
Input size \(|x|\) is measured in bits under a fixed encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_A(n)=O(f(n))\) exactly under the stated eventual uniform upper bound.

children.title: Practical Solver Complexity
children.top_down_role: Resource behavior encountered on representative solver workloads.

assumptions_latex: The solver, hardware, resource limits, and instance-size encoding are fixed.
\(\mu_n\) or the finite benchmark set \(S\) is explicitly specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{A,\alpha}(n)\) and \(\operatorname{PAR}_k(A,S,\tau)\) are reproducible practical-cost summaries only relative to the stated workload, platform, and timeout convention.

notation.meaning: Instance distribution at encoded size n.
Penalized average runtime with penalty factor k and timeout tau.
Instances solved by A within timeout tau.
Instances not solved by A within timeout tau.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional and timeout-censored runtime representations for a fixed benchmark population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_n\) be a probability distribution over solver instances of encoded size \(n\), let \(R_A(x)\in[0,\infty]\) be solver \(A\)'s uncensored runtime, and let \(0<\alpha<1\). A distributional practical-complexity summary is the runtime quantile \(Q_{A,\alpha}(n)=\inf\{t\ge0:\Pr_{x\sim\mu_n}[R_A(x)\le t]\ge\alpha\}\). For a finite benchmark set \(S\), timeout \(\tau>0\), and penalty factor \(k\ge1\), let \(S_{\mathrm{solved}}=\{x\in S:R_A(x)\le\tau\}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{timeout}}=S\setminus S_{\mathrm{solved}}\). Then \(\operatorname{PAR}_k(A,S,\tau)=|S|^{-1}\bigl(\sum_{x\in S_{\mathrm{solved}}}R_A(x)+|S_{\mathrm{timeout}}|k\tau\bigr)\), so every timeout receives cost \(k\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Practical solver complexity can be summarized by runtime quantiles for a specified workload or by a penalized average that assigns a fixed multiple of the timeout to every timed-out benchmark instance.
knowledge_statements.title: Practical Solver Complexity

children.title: Theory–Practice Complexity Gaps
children.top_down_role: Structural reasons that practical behavior diverges from worst-case expectations.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory–Practice Complexity Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative comparison between worst-case and workload-quantile runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For solver \(A\), worst-case runtime \(W_A(n)\), workload distribution \(\mu_n\), and runtime quantile \(Q_{A,\alpha}(n)>0\), define the theory–practice gap ratio by \(G_{A,\alpha}(n)=W_A(n)/Q_{A,\alpha}(n)\). A growing ratio means that worst-case behavior increasingly exceeds the selected practical quantile; it does not establish that the worst-case bound is loose, because rare instances may attain it. Comparisons are meaningful only when both quantities use the same solver, size encoding, computational resources, and cost unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The worst-case-to-quantile runtime ratio measures a theory–practice gap, but a large ratio does not invalidate the worst-case bound.
assumptions_latex: \(W_A(n)\) and \(Q_{A,\alpha}(n)\) use the same input encoding and runtime model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_{A,\alpha}(n)\to\infty\) expresses an asymptotically widening worst-case versus workload-quantile gap.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio is internally coherent and the cautions are appropriate, but it is presented as a local formalization rather than a sourced standard property.
